questions.stem: Which one of the following is responsible for controlling the flow of bits between memory and controllers with no need for a constant intervention from the CPU?
questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 29

answer.explanation: DMA transfers a block directly between device and memory; the CPU supplies setup information and receives completion notification, rather than moving every word (PDF pp.107–108). This precisely meets the absence of constant intervention. A generic device controller alone does not establish DMA capability.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Disk fragmenting is not the block-transfer mechanism described on pp.107–108.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The corrupted name “Memo, manager” does not identify the DMA mechanism on p.107.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An I/O controller can notify the CPU under interrupt I/O; that still leaves CPU data movement (p.106).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct transfers and only beginning/end CPU involvement are explicit on p.108.

evidence.quote: Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.
DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
7.10 Direct Memory Access (DMA)
Interrupt driven and programmed I/O require active CPU intervention.
Transfer rate is limited
CPU is tied up DMA is the solution for these problems
Direct Memory Access is capabilities provided by some computer bus architectures that
allow data to be sent directly from an attached device (such as a disk drive) to the memory on
the computer’s motherboard. The microprocessor (CPU) is freed from involvement with the
data transfer, thus speeding up overall computer operation.

module_refs.quote:
When the CPU wishes to read or write a block of data, it issues a command to the DMA

 Device address
 Starting address of memory block for data
 Amount of data to be transferred The CPU carries on with other work.
 Thus DMA controller steals the CPU‟s work of I/O operation.
 The DMA module transfers the entire block of data
 One word at a time, directly to or from memory, without going through CPU.
When the transfer is complete, DMA controller sends interrupt when finished Thus CPU
is involved only at the beginning and at the end of the transfer.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Programmed I/O :With Programmed I/O, data are exchanged between the CPU and
the I/O module. The CPU executes a program that gives it direct control of the I/O
operation, including sensing device status, sending a read or write command and
transferring data. When CPU issues a command to I/O module, it must wait until I/O
operation is complete. If the CPU is faster than I/O module, there is wastage of CPU
time. The I/O module does not take any further action to alert CPU. That is it doesn’t
interrupt CPU. Hence it is the responsibility of the CPU to periodically check the
status of the I/O module until it finds that the operation is complete. The sequences of
actions that take place with programmed I/O are:
 CPU requests I/O operation
 I/O module performs operation
 I/O module sets status bits
 CPU checks status bits periodically
 I/O module does not inform CPU directly
 I/O module does not interrupt CPU

Using Program-controlled I/O requires continuous involvement of the processor in the I/O
activities. It is desirable to avoid wasting processor execution time. An alternative is for the
CPU to issue an I/O command to a module and then go on other work. The I/O module will

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a communication pathway connecting transmitting signals in binary digits between two or more devices?
questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 44

answer.explanation: The common bus is a set of shared lines used to transfer binary information among registers (PDF p.40). The structural definitions distinguish storage and processing components from their communication mechanism (p.6).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Main memory stores data; it is an endpoint (p.6).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Registers store bits, rather than naming the pathway (p.35).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU processes and controls; it is a communicating component (p.6).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A bus supplies common bit lines and selection controls (p.40).

evidence.quote: A bus is a set of common signal lines used to transfer binary information among connected units.
The CPU contains an ALU, control unit and registers; a microcontroller is a complete integrated control system, not another mandatory CPU subunit.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
4.2 Bus and Memory Transfers
A typical computer has many registers, and paths must be provided to transfer information
from one register to another. An efficient way for transferring information between registers
in a multiple-register configuration is a common bus system. A bus structure consists of a set
of common lines, one for each bit of a register. Control signals determine which register the
bus selects during each particular register transfer.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
There are four main structural components:
 Central processing unit (CPU): Controls the operation of the computer and performs its
data processing functions; often simply referred to as processor.
 Main memory: Stores data.
 I/O: Moves data between the computer and its external environment.
 System interconnection: Some mechanism that provides for communication among
CPU, main memory, and I/O.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module

3.9 Registers
 A register is a group of flip-flops with each flip- flop capable of storing one bit of
information.
 A register is a digital circuit used within the CPU to store one or more bits of data.
 An n-bit register has a group of n flip-flops and is capable of storing n bits of binary
information.
 In addition to Flip-Flops, it may have combinational gates that perform certain data
processing.
 Two basic types of registers are commonly used: parallel registers and shift registers.

questions.stem: Which memory is characterized by the need for periodic change in order to maintain data storage?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 56

answer.explanation: Interpret “periodic change” as periodic charge refreshing: capacitor charge leaks, so DRAM needs refresh (PDF p.80). This is different from SRAM power retention and nonvolatile secondary storage (p.91).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SRAM uses flip-flops and holds data while powered (p.80), without the stated charge refresh.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DRAM capacitor discharge explicitly requires periodic refreshing (p.80).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Disk is nonvolatile secondary storage (p.91), not capacitor-refresh RAM.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Tape is also nonvolatile secondary storage (p.91), not refresh RAM.

evidence.quote: SRAM uses powered bistable storage: fast and costly per bit, without periodic refresh.
DRAM stores charge and requires refresh: denser and commonly used for main memory.
It does not need continuous power to preserve stored bits.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
DYNAMIC RAM (DRAM)
is made with cells that store data as charge on capacitors. The presence or absence of charge
in a capacitor is interpreted as a binary 1 or 0. Because capacitors have a natural tendency to
discharge, DRAMs require periodic charge refreshing to maintain data storage.
STATIC RAM (SRAM)
In a SRAM, binary values are stored using traditional flip-flop logic-gate. A static RAM will
hold its data as long as power is supplied to it. Static RAM’s are faster than dynamic RAM’s.

 This kind of memory is large, slow and inexpensive.
 It is non-volatile storage media i.e. the contents are not erased when the power is
switched off.
 Magnetic disk, Magnetic tape and optical disk are the examples of secondary storage.

questions.stem: In the ordinary HDD model, which statement is incorrect? Read/write refers to accessing sectors on the current track; seeking to another track is a separate operation.

options.label: A
options.text: Data is arranged in sectors within tracks

options.label: B
options.text: The head stays over the selected track while its sectors rotate beneath it

options.label: C
options.text: Its data is organized in tracks

options.label: D
options.text: It needs continuous power to keep bit contents

questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 60

answer.text: It needs continuous power to keep bit contents
answer.explanation: An HDD records magnetic patterns in sectors arranged on tracks. During access to a selected track, rotation brings sectors under the head; seeking moves the head radially to another track. The medium retains its magnetic contents without continuous power, so the claimed power requirement is false. Power is needed to operate the drive, but that differs from power needed merely to retain the stored bits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Sectors are subdivisions of tracks in the stated HDD organization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This describes track-local access; a separate seek changes which track is under the head.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Magnetic disk data is organized on tracks, so this statement is true.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An HDD is nonvolatile: retaining stored patterns does not require continuous power.

evidence.quote: An HDD stores magnetic patterns on tracks divided into sectors; reads/writes access addressed blocks while platters rotate.
A head normally stays over a track while reading but moves radially for seeks.
It does not need continuous power to preserve stored bits.

questions.stem: Which listed circuit category requires stored state so that output can depend on past input behavior as well as present inputs?

options.label: C
options.text: A two-input AND gate with no feedback

options.label: D
options.text: A combinational multiplexer with no storage

questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 93

answer.explanation: A sequential circuit contains state that preserves information about prior behavior. A combinational circuit computes its outputs from current inputs after propagation delay. The specified AND gate and multiplexer are combinational examples without storage or feedback. They therefore do not require remembered state, while the sequential-circuit category does. This distinction concerns logical state, not whether physical propagation takes time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Combinational output depends on current inputs rather than stored history.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sequential circuits retain state and can make output depend on past behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The specified AND gate computes a truth function of its present inputs without storage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The specified multiplexer selects a present data input; it has no stored logical state.

evidence.quote: A combinational output depends on present inputs after propagation delay.
Adders, multiplexers, demultiplexers, encoders and decoders have no stored logical state.
A sequential circuit depends on stored state as well as inputs; registers, counters and flip-flops are examples.
AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR is 1 if any input is 1.

module_refs.quote:

signals applied to the inputs.

 Sequential circuits consist of a combinational circuit and some memory elements. The

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module

1.4 Combinational Circuits
 A combinational circuit is an interconnected set of gates whose output at any time is a

input is followed almost immediately by the appearance of the output, with only gate
delays. In general terms, a combinational circuit consists of n binary inputs and m
binary outputs.

questions.stem: In computers, subtraction is carried out generally by __________.

sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 36
Computer Science Exit Exam · Sene 2016 · Question 20-3
Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 239

answer.explanation: Subtraction is described as complementation plus addition: add one to the inverted subtrahend, then add that two’s complement to the minuend (PDF p.42). Hence R1 + (~R2+1) represents R1−R2 within the register width.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One’s complement alone omits the added 1 in p.42’s subtraction procedure.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The inversion-plus-one subtrahend is exactly two’s complement (p.42).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The cited procedure does not use separate sign and magnitude arithmetic.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The cited general register subtraction is not BCD digit subtraction.

questions.stem: An operation performed on the contents of a register is known as
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 38

answer.explanation: An elementary operation on information stored in one or more registers is explicitly defined as a micro operation (PDF p.38). An instruction code tells the computer what operation to execute, while registers are the storage objects (pp.35,47).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An instruction code specifies work; it is not the elementary register operation itself (p.47).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Matches the exact definition and examples shift, count, clear, load (p.38).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Accumulator denotes a processing register, not the operation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A register stores the information being operated on (p.35).

evidence.quote: A microoperation is one elementary operation on register contents.
An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Digital modules are best defined by the registers they contain and the operations that are
performed on the data stored in them. The operations executed on data stored in registers are
called micro operations. A micro operation is an elementary operation performed on the
information stored in one or more registers.
Examples of micro operation are shift, count, clear, and load.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
An Instruction Code is a group of bits that instructs the computer to perform a specific
operation. It is usually divided into parts, each having its own particular interpretation. The
most basic part of an instruction code is its operation part. The operation code of an
instruction is a group of bits that defines such operations as Add, Subtract, Multiply, Shift
and Complement. The operation part of an instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed. This operation must be performed on some data stored in processor registers or
in memory. An instruction must specify not only the operation but also the registers or the
memory words where the operands are to be found.

questions.stem: Which one is true about RISC computers?

options.label: A
options.text: RISC are with few numbers of registers when compared to CISC

options.label: B
options.text: RISC use complex and efficient machine instructions when compared to CISC

options.label: C
options.text: RISC is with hardwired control unit with pipelining processing

options.label: D
options.text: RISC uses extensive addressing capabilities for memory operations

questions.hint: Compare textbook design tendencies without turning them into guarantees about every processor.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 39

answer.text: RISC is with hardwired control unit with pipelining processing
answer.explanation: RISC characteristics explicitly include hardwired control, many registers, few addressing modes and an efficient pipeline (PDF p.77). These jointly support C and contradict the reversed CISC-like descriptions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A reverses the relatively large register count on p.77.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Complex instructions are the CISC characteristic (p.78), whereas RISC has few, easily decoded instructions (p.77).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both hardwired control and efficient pipeline are explicitly listed (p.77).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: RISC has relatively few addressing modes and memory access limited to loads/stores (p.77).

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: C is supported, so “None” fails.

evidence.quote: The textbook RISC design pairs a relatively large register set, load/store access and easily decoded instructions with hardwired rather than microprogrammed control and an efficient pipeline.
CISC commonly supplies more complex operations, richer addressing modes and variable lengths.

• A relatively large number of registers in the processor
• Use overlapped register windows to speed up procedure call and return
• Efficient instruction pipeline

5.11. Central Processing Unit.
The part of the computer that performs the bulk of data processing operations is called the
Central processing unit and is referred to as the CPU. The CPU is made up of three major
parts The register set stores intermediate data used during the execution of the instructions.
The Arithmetic and Logic unit (ALU) performs the required micro-operations for executing
the instructions. The control unit supervises the transfer of information among the registers

performs a variety of functions dictated by the type of instructions that are incorporated in the
computer. Computer architecture is sometimes defined as the computer structure and
behavior as seen by the programmer that uses machine language instructions. This includes
the instruction formats, addressing modes, the instruction sets and the general organizations
of the CPU registers

questions.stem: After CPU setup, which transfer method moves a block between an I/O device and memory without the CPU copying each data word?
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 41

answer.explanation: DMA assigns the block movement to a controller after the CPU configures the transfer. Polling and ordinary interrupt-driven I/O still make the CPU execute item transfers. A software interrupt is an instruction-requested control transfer to a handler, not a block-copy engine. CPU setup and completion handling remain part of DMA; bypass refers specifically to avoiding CPU copying for every word.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A software interrupt requests handler execution; it does not itself move a block directly between device and memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The interrupt handler still uses CPU execution to service the device and move items.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The CPU checks status and moves items itself in polled I/O.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The DMA controller performs the block transfer after setup, avoiding per-word CPU copies.

evidence.quote: Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.
DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.
A software interrupt is deliberately requested by an instruction.

module_refs.quote:
In the programming examples of the previous chapter, we have shown that memory locations
are needed for storing pointers, counters, return addresses, temporary results and partial
product during multiplication. Having to refer to memory locations for such applications is
time consuming because memory access is the most time consuming operation in a computer.
It is more convenient and more efficient to store these intermediate values in processor
register. When a large number of registers are included in the CPU, It is most efficient to
connect them through a common bus system. The registers communicate with each other not
only for direct data transfers, but also while performing various micro operations.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.3 Cache Memory
Cache memory is a small, high-speed RAM buffer located between the CPU and main
memory.
Cache memory holds a copy of the instructions (instruction cache) or data (operand or data
cache) currently being used by the CPU.
The main purpose of a cache is to accelerate your computer while keeping the price of the
computer low.
• The cache is the fastest component in the memory hierarchy and approaches the speed of
CPU component
• When CPU needs to access memory, the cache is examined
• If the word is found in the cache, it is read from the fast memory
• If the word addressed by the CPU is not found in the cache, the main memory is accessed
to read the word
• When the CPU refers to memory and finds the word in cache, it is said to produce a hit
• Otherwise, it is a miss

Data transfer instruction.
Data transfer instructions move data from place to place in the computer to another without
changing the data content. The most common transfers are between memory and processor
registers, between processor register and input or output, and between the processor registers
themselves. Table 5-5 gives lists of eight data transfer instructions used in many computers.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Immediate Mode: In this mode the operand is specified in the instruction itself. In other
words, an immediate mode instruction has an operand field rather than an address field. The
operand field contains the actual operand to be used in conjunction with the operation
specified in the instruction. Immediate mode instructions are useful for initializing registers
to a constant value.
When the address field specifies a processor register, the instruction is said to be in the
register mode.
Register Mode: In this mode the operands are in registers that reside within the CPU. The
particular register is selected from a register field in the instruction. A k-bit field can specify
any of the 2k registers.
Register Indirect Mode: In this mode the instruction specifies a register in the CPU whose
contents give the address of the operand in memory. In other words, the selected register
contains the address of the operand rather than the operand itself. Before using a register
indirect mode instruction, the programmer must ensure that the memory address of the
operand is placed in the processor register with a previous instruction. A reference to the
register is then equivalent to specifying a memory address. The advantage of the register
indirect mode instruction is that the address field of the instruction uses fewer bits to select a
register than would have been required to specify a memory address directly.

Digital modules are best defined by the registers they contain and the operations that are
performed on the data stored in them. The operations executed on data stored in registers are
called micro operations. A micro operation is an elementary operation performed on the
information stored in one or more registers.
Examples of micro operation are shift, count, clear, and load.

operand is placed in the processor register with a previous instruction. A reference to the
register is then equivalent to specifying a memory address. The advantage of the register
indirect mode instruction is that the address field of the instruction uses fewer bits to select a
register than would have been required to specify a memory address directly.

choices.label: B

choices.explanation: 32 multiplies AL by CL, whereas the explicit operand is BH, not CL.

questions.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 30

answer.text: All listed categories are forms of computer design/architecture in the broad wording.
answer.explanation: COA01 calls microarchitecture the internal processor design, while COA02 contrasts Harvard and Von Neumann memory organizations. The broad phrase type of computer architecture encompasses all three usages, although they describe different abstraction levels. The comprehensive answer is therefore all of the mentioned. No single named option covers the entire set of valid architectural categories.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Microarchitecture is a valid internal-design category, but this alone omits the two valid memory organizations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Harvard is a valid architecture category, but selecting it alone excludes the other valid categories.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Von Neumann is valid, but the broad question also admits microarchitecture and Harvard organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three names describe architectural design categories, though they operate at different abstraction levels.

evidence.quote: Microarchitecture names the internal processor design.
In the textbook Von Neumann model, instructions and data share an addressed memory system; the CPU normally advances sequentially unless control flow changes.
Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Computer architecture: refers to those attributes of a system visible to a programmer or,
put another way, those attributes that have a direct impact on the logical execution of a
program. Examples of architectural attributes include the instruction set, the number of bits
used to represent various data types (e.g., numbers, characters), I/O mechanisms, and
techniques for addressing memory.
Computer organization refers to the operational units and their interconnections that realize
the architectural specifications. Organizational attributes include those hardware details
transparent to the programmer, such as control signals; interfaces between the computer and
peripherals; and the memory technology used.

questions.stem: Which one is not a combinational circuit?
questions.hint: Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 31

answer.explanation: A register is a group of state-holding flip-flops (PDF p.35). Sequential circuits retain past information (p.15), whereas code/routing combinational circuits transform current inputs (pp.31,33–34). Thus register is the non-combinational choice.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encoder maps the active input into a binary code (p.34); no stored state is part of this described mapping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Decoder selects an output based on the input pattern (p.33).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiplexer is explicitly combinational (p.31).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Demultiplexer routes one input to a selected output (p.33), a present-input routing function.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Register contains storage flip-flops and retains state (p.35).

evidence.quote: A combinational output depends on present inputs after propagation delay.
A sequential circuit depends on stored state as well as inputs; registers, counters and flip-flops are examples.

module_refs.quote:

 A register is a group of flip-flops with each flip- flop capable of storing one bit of
information.
 A register is a digital circuit used within the CPU to store one or more bits of data.
 An n-bit register has a group of n flip-flops and is capable of storing n bits of binary

 In addition to Flip-Flops, it may have combinational gates that perform certain data

module_refs.quote:
3.7 Decoders
 A decoder is a combinational circuit with a number of output lines, only one of which
is selected at any time, depending on the pattern of input lines.
 In general, a decoder has n inputs and 2n
outputs.
 Decoders find many uses in digital computers.
 One example is address decoding.
 The other is binary-to- octal conversion.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
3.8 Encoders
 An encoder is a digital circuit that performs the inverse operation of a decoder.
 An encoder has 2n
(or less) input lines and n output lines. The output lines generate
the binary code corresponding to the input value.
 An example of an encoder is the octal-to-binary encoder.

module_refs.quote:

 Multiplexer is a combinational circuit that receives binary information from one of 2n

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
1.4 Combinational Circuits
 A combinational circuit is an interconnected set of gates whose output at any time is a

delays. In general terms, a combinational circuit consists of n binary inputs and m
binary outputs.

questions.stem:
In a _________ cache organization, cache permits data to be stored in any cache
block.
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 32

answer.explanation: Associative cache stores an address with each data item and searches by content (PDF p.87), rather than constraining a block to a single index. Set association retains index constraints (p.88). Fully associative is therefore the any-block placement organization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct mapping has fixed index conflicts (p.88), so does not allow arbitrary block placement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Set association allows multiple entries under the same index, not any block anywhere (p.88).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Address/content pairs searched associatively permit the unrestricted mapping described (p.87).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct and set mappings are restricted, so not all satisfy the claim.

evidence.quote: Direct mapping uses line=block mod L.
Fully associative placement permits any line.
A W-way set-associative cache has S=L/W sets and set=block mod S; any of W ways in that set may hold the block.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Associative Mapping
 An associative mapping uses an associative memory.
 This memory is being accessed using its contents.
 Associative memory is expensive compared to RAM
 Each line of cache memory will accommodate the address (main memory) and the
contents of that address from the main memory.
 That is why this memory is also called Content Addressable Memory (CAM). It
allows each block of main memory to be stored in the cache.
A CPU address of 15 bits is places in the argument register and the associative memory us
searched for a matching address
• If the address is found, the corresponding 12bits data is read and sent to the CPU
• If not, the main memory is accessed for the word
If the cache is full, an address-data pair must be displaced to make room for a pair that is
needed and not presently in the cache

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Set Associative Mapping
That is the easy control of the direct mapping cache and the more flexible mapping of the
fully associative cache.
In set associative mapping, each cache location can have more than one pair of tag + data
items.
That is more than one pair of tag and data are residing at the same location of cache memory.
If one cache location is holding two pair of tag + data items, that is called 2-way set
associative mapping.
The disadvantage of direct mapping is that two words with the same index in their address
but with different tag values cannot reside in cache memory at the same time
Set-Associative Mapping is an improvement over the direct-mapping in that each word of
cache can store two or more word of memory under the same index address

questions.stem:
Which one used to translate virtual addresses into physical addresses when we are
implementing the concept of Virtual memory?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 33

answer.explanation: COA27 states that the MMU translates virtual/logical addresses into physical addresses using page tables and often a TLB. LRU and FIFO instead choose replacement victims, as described in COA26. Neither replacement policy performs address translation. Consequently the MMU is the single component matching the requested virtual-memory translation role; the all alternative incorrectly includes two different mechanisms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: LRU chooses a least-recently-used replacement victim; it does not translate virtual addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FIFO selects the earliest inserted replacement victim, rather than computing physical addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The MMU performs virtual-to-physical address translation using the translation structures described in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Only the MMU translates addresses; LRU and FIFO are replacement policies.

evidence.quote: The MMU translates virtual/logical addresses to physical addresses, using page tables and often a TLB of recent translations.
FIFO evicts the earliest inserted line; LRU evicts the least recently accessed line.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Concept of Virtual Memory
A programmer can write a program which requires more memory space than the capacity of
the main memory. Such a program is executed by virtual memory technique.
The program is stored in the secondary memory. The memory management unit (MMU)
transfers the currently needed part of the program from the secondary memory to the main
memory for execution.
This to and fro movement of instructions and data (parts of a program) between the main
memory and the secondary memory is called Swapping.
Address Space And Memory Space.
Virtual address is the address used by the programmer and the set of such addresses is called
the address space or virtual memory.
An address in main memory is called a location or physical address. The set of such
locations in main memory is called the memory space or physical memory.
CPU generated logical address consisting of a logical page number plus the location within
that page (x).

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
It must be mapped onto an actual (physical) main memory address by the operating system
using mapper.
If the page is present in the main memory, CPU gets the required data from the main
memory.
If the mapper detects that the requested page is not present in main memory, a page fault
occurs and the page must be read from secondary storage into a page frame in main memory.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.3.2 Replacement Algorithms of Cache Memory
Replacement algorithms are used when there are no available space in a cache in which to
place a data. Four of the most common cache replacement algorithms are described below:
Least Recently Used (LRU):
The LRU algorithm selects for replacement the item that has been least recently used by the
CPU.
First-In-First-Out (FIFO):
The FIFO algorithm selects for replacement the item that has been in the cache from the
longest time.

questions.stem: In a ________ bus, flow is only one-way from the CPU to memory.
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 34

answer.explanation: In the CPU-master model, CPU address registers identify the memory location (PDF pp.82–83), while data supports reads and writes (p.105) and control/status includes messages from both sides (pp.102–103). This makes A the specific one-way address path.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The CPU supplies the memory address (pp.82–83).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Read and write data travel in opposite directions (p.105).

choices.label: C

Data transfer between the main memory and the CPU register takes place through two
registers namely MAR (memory address register) and MDR (memory data register). If MAR
is k bits long and MDR is n bits long, the main memory unit can contain up to 2k addressable
locations.

During a “memory cycle‟ n bits of data are transferred between main memory and CPU.

A computer system is equipped with a hierarchy of memory subsystems. There are several

questions.stem: Which Shift register type used to act as a delay element?
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 36

answer.explanation: The shift register accepts/transfers data serially and moves each bit one position per clock, emitting the rightmost bit (PDF p.36). With serial input and serial output, an n-stage register delays the stream by n shifts. This derivation identifies SISO under the usual stream-delay meaning.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Serial input traverses storage stages to serial output, producing the clock-count delay (p.36).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Parallel input/serial output serializes a loaded word; it does not preserve the incoming serial stream in the described way.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Serial input/parallel output exposes the stored bits together rather than the delayed serial stream.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Not all listed I/O forms implement the same serial-stream delay.

evidence.quote: SISO shift registers delay serial streams; SIPO collects a word and PISO serializes a parallel word.
A flip-flop stores one bit while powered.

Shift Register

questions.stem: Which one of them is a Universal Logic Gates?
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 38

answer.explanation: Figure 1.2 on PDF p.7 gives NAND as NOT(A AND B). Tie its inputs to obtain NOT A; NAND followed by that inverter gives AND; applying NAND to inverted inputs gives OR, as can be checked against the same truth tables. Thus NAND alone can build the basic AND/OR/NOT set.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: NAND supplies inversion by tying inputs and then AND/OR by composition (p.7, Figure 1.2).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: XOR alone maps all-zero inputs to zero; it cannot supply the inverter required by Figure 1.2.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: AND alone also preserves zero and cannot produce NOT using only AND gates.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NOT only complements one input; it cannot combine independent input variables into AND/OR.

evidence.quote: NAND and NOR are each universal: feeding the same input to both inputs constructs NOT; combine complemented gates to construct AND or OR.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Binary information in digital computers represented by physical quantities called signal.
The fundamental building block of all digital logic circuits is the gate. Logical functions are
implemented by the interconnection of gates. A gate is an electronic circuit that produces an
output signal that is a simple Boolean operation on its input signals. The basic gates used in
digital logic are AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, and XOR. Each gate is defined in three
ways: graphic symbol, algebraic notation, and truth table. Note that the inversion (NOT)
operation is indicated by a circle.

questions.stem: Which textbook architecture model stores instructions and data in a shared addressed memory system?
questions.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
sources: Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 39

answer.explanation: The Von Neumann model uses a shared addressed memory system for instructions and data. Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths. Microarchitecture names an internal implementation, while system design is broader than the particular stored-program memory model requested. The revised stem asks about a defining memory relationship rather than claiming that all modern computers use one exclusive organization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Microarchitecture describes internal processor implementation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Von Neumann uses the described shared addressed memory model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: System design is broader than this named memory model.

evidence.quote: In the textbook Von Neumann model, instructions and data share an addressed memory system; the CPU normally advances sequentially unless control flow changes.
Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths.
Microarchitecture names the internal processor design.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The simplest way to organize a computer is to have one processor register and an instruction
code format with two parts. The first part of instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed and the second specifies an address. The memory address tells the control where
to find an operand in memory. This operand is read from memory and used as the data to be
operated on together with the data stored in processor register. Instructions are stored in one
section of memory and data in another. The operation is performed with memory operands
and the content of AC. Figure 5-1 below depicts this type of organization.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Computer instructions are usually stored in consecutive memory locations and executed
sequentially one at a time. The control reads an instruction from specific address in memory
and executes it. It then continues by reading the next instruction in sequence and executes it
and so on. This type of instruction sequencing needs a counter to calculate the address of the
next instruction after execution of the current instruction is completed. It is also necessary to
provide a register in a control unit for storing the instruction code after it is read from the
memory. The data register (DR) holds the operand read from memory. The accumulator (AC)
register is a general purpose processing register. The instructions read from memory are
placed in instruction register (IR). The temporary register (TR) is used for holding temporary
data during the processing.

questions.stem: In a design connecting a processor-side bus segment to an unlike peripheral bus segment, which hardware category provides the necessary bridge or interface logic?
questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 6

answer.explanation: Unlike bus segments need bridge or controller logic to adapt their interfaces and coordinate transfers. PCI names a peripheral expansion interconnect, while SCSI names a storage connection; neither alone identifies the adapting component. Multibus names a bus rather than the requested bridge category. The revised topology and component requirement make the interface-logic choice definite without assuming a particular processor bus or expansion standard.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SCSI is a storage-connection standard rather than a bridge component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: PCI names an expansion interconnect rather than the adapting logic.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: PCI is a peripheral expansion interconnect, not a disk protocol; connecting unlike bus segments requires suitable bridge/controller logic.
SATA is a storage interface; legacy IDE/PATA and SCSI represent other storage connections, while iSCSI carries SCSI commands over IP.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
4.2 Bus and Memory Transfers
A typical computer has many registers, and paths must be provided to transfer information
from one register to another. An efficient way for transferring information between registers
in a multiple-register configuration is a common bus system. A bus structure consists of a set
of common lines, one for each bit of a register. Control signals determine which register the
bus selects during each particular register transfer.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
7.10 Direct Memory Access (DMA)
Interrupt driven and programmed I/O require active CPU intervention.
Transfer rate is limited
CPU is tied up DMA is the solution for these problems
Direct Memory Access is capabilities provided by some computer bus architectures that
allow data to be sent directly from an attached device (such as a disk drive) to the memory on
the computer’s motherboard. The microprocessor (CPU) is freed from involvement with the
data transfer, thus speeding up overall computer operation.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
When the CPU wishes to read or write a block of data, it issues a command to the DMA
module and gives following information: CPU tells DMA controller:
 Whether to read or write
 Device address
 Starting address of memory block for data
 Amount of data to be transferred The CPU carries on with other work.
 Thus DMA controller steals the CPU‟s work of I/O operation.
 The DMA module transfers the entire block of data
 One word at a time, directly to or from memory, without going through CPU.
When the transfer is complete, DMA controller sends interrupt when finished Thus CPU
is involved only at the beginning and at the end of the transfer.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
I. Fetch the instruction
Initially, the program counter PC is loaded with the address of the first instruction in the
program and SC is cleared to 0, providing a decoded timing signal T0. After each clock
pulse, SC is incremented by one, so that the timing signals go through a sequence T0, T1, T2
and so on. Since the address lines of the memory unit are hardwired to AR, address of the
instruction to be fetched must first be placed in AR. Thus the first register transfer in an
instruction cycle should be transferring the content of PC (address of the instruction to be
brought in for execution) to AR
T0: AR ← PC
Bus selects PC, LD(AR) = 1. Next the current instruction is brought from memory into IR
and PC is incremented
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. Bus selects RAM, Memory read is set, LD(IR) = 1,
INR(PC) = 1
II. Decode the instruction
T2: D0, ... , D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)
Therefore, micro-operations for the fetch and decode phases can be specified by the
following register transfer statements.
T0: AR ← PC
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2: D0, …, D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)

7.10 Direct Memory Access (DMA)
Interrupt driven and programmed I/O require active CPU intervention.
Transfer rate is limited

Direct Memory Access is capabilities provided by some computer bus architectures that

 Starting address of memory block for data
 Amount of data to be transferred The CPU carries on with other work.
 Thus DMA controller steals the CPU‟s work of I/O operation.
 The DMA module transfers the entire block of data
 One word at a time, directly to or from memory, without going through CPU.

Asynchronous data transfer

a common pulse generator. Two units such as cpu and an I/O are designed independently of
each other, if the register in the interface share a common clock with the cpu registers, the
transfer between the two units is called to be synchronous.in most case the internal timing in
each unit is independent from the other in that each uses its own private clock for internal
register.in such cases the two units are said to be asynchronous to each other. This approach
is widely used in most computers systems.

Interrupt Driven I/O.

activities. It is desirable to avoid wasting processor execution time. An alternative is for the
CPU to issue an I/O command to a module and then go on other work. The I/O module will
then interrupt the CPU requesting service when it is ready to exchange data with the CPU.
The CPU will then execute the data transfer and then resumes its former processing. Based on
the use of interrupts, this technique improves the utilization of the processor. With Interrupt
driven I/O, the CPU issues a command to I/O module and it does not wait until I/O operation
is complete but instead continues to execute other instructions. When I/O module has
completed its work it interrupts the CPU. An interrupt is more than a simple mechanism for

program to another to be initiated by an event that is external to a computer. Execution of the

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Programmed I/O :With Programmed I/O, data are exchanged between the CPU and
the I/O module. The CPU executes a program that gives it direct control of the I/O
operation, including sensing device status, sending a read or write command and
transferring data. When CPU issues a command to I/O module, it must wait until I/O
operation is complete. If the CPU is faster than I/O module, there is wastage of CPU
time. The I/O module does not take any further action to alert CPU. That is it doesn’t
interrupt CPU. Hence it is the responsibility of the CPU to periodically check the
status of the I/O module until it finds that the operation is complete. The sequences of
actions that take place with programmed I/O are:
 CPU requests I/O operation
 I/O module performs operation
 I/O module sets status bits
 CPU checks status bits periodically
 I/O module does not inform CPU directly
 I/O module does not interrupt CPU

module_refs.quote:
An Instruction Code is a group of bits that instructs the computer to perform a specific
operation. It is usually divided into parts, each having its own particular interpretation. The
most basic part of an instruction code is its operation part. The operation code of an
instruction is a group of bits that defines such operations as Add, Subtract, Multiply, Shift
and Complement. The operation part of an instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed. This operation must be performed on some data stored in processor registers or
in memory. An instruction must specify not only the operation but also the registers or the
memory words where the operands are to be found.

capabilities for the computer. The data manipulation instructions in a typical computer are

1. Arithmetic instruction
2. Logical and bit manipulation
3. Shift instruction
a. Arithmetic Instruction
The four basic arithmetic operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
Most computers provide instructions for all four operations. Some small computers have only
addition and possibly subtraction instructions. The multiplication and division must then be
generated by means of software subroutines.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Binary information in digital computers represented by physical quantities called signal.
The fundamental building block of all digital logic circuits is the gate. Logical functions are
implemented by the interconnection of gates. A gate is an electronic circuit that produces an
output signal that is a simple Boolean operation on its input signals. The basic gates used in
digital logic are AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, and XOR. Each gate is defined in three

operation is indicated by a circle.

information stored in one or more registers.
Examples of micro operation are shift, count, clear, and load.

module_refs.quote:
Computer instructions are usually stored in consecutive memory locations and executed
sequentially one at a time. The control reads an instruction from specific address in memory
and executes it. It then continues by reading the next instruction in sequence and executes it
and so on. This type of instruction sequencing needs a counter to calculate the address of the
next instruction after execution of the current instruction is completed. It is also necessary to
provide a register in a control unit for storing the instruction code after it is read from the
memory. The data register (DR) holds the operand read from memory. The accumulator (AC)
register is a general purpose processing register. The instructions read from memory are
placed in instruction register (IR). The temporary register (TR) is used for holding temporary
data during the processing.

module_refs.quote:
5.19 CISC Instruction:
CISC refers to Complex Instruction Set Computer
CISC characteristic
• Large number of instructions – typically from 100 to 250 instructions
• Some instructions that perform specialized tasks and are used infrequently
• A large variety of addressing modes – typically from 5 to 20 different modes
• Variable length instruction formats
• Instructions that manipulate operands in memory RISC characteristics

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
A RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) processor pipeline operates in much the same
way, although the stages in the pipeline are different. While different processors have
different numbers of steps, they have basically variations of these five steps:
1. fetch instructions from memory
2. read registers and decode the instruction
3. execute the instruction or calculate an address
4. access an operand in data memory
5. write the result into a register
The length of the pipeline is dependent on the length of the longest step. Because RISC
instructions are simpler than those used in pre-RISC processors (now called CISC, or
Complex Instruction Set Computer), they are more conducive to pipelining. While CISC
instructions varied in length, RISC instructions are all the same length and can be fetched in a
single operation. Ideally, each of the stages in a RISC processor pipeline should take 1 clock
cycle so that the processor finishes an instruction each clock cycle and averages one cycle per
instruction (CPI). Among the characteristics attributed to RISC is its ability to use an efficient
instruction pipeline.

Cache memory is a small, high-speed RAM buffer located between the CPU and main

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
There are four main structural components:
 Central processing unit (CPU): Controls the operation of the computer and performs its
data processing functions; often simply referred to as processor.
 Main memory: Stores data.
 I/O: Moves data between the computer and its external environment.
 System interconnection: Some mechanism that provides for communication among
CPU, main memory, and I/O.

questions.stem: A stack organized computer uses instruction of
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Mock exam 1 · Question 7

answer.explanation: For stack arithmetic the operands are implicit on top of stack, so ADD and MUL require no address field (PDF p.69). This is the zero-address organization. PUSH/POP still use explicit addresses; the answer concerns arithmetic operation instructions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Zero-address ADD/MUL is explicit (p.69).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two-address instructions instead explicitly name register/memory operands; stack arithmetic does not (pp.67–69).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Index addressing is an effective-address mechanism, not the stack operand-count format.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Indirect addressing locates an address through memory (p.72); it is not the stack arithmetic format.

evidence.quote: Zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands.
A stack is last-in, first-out.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
5.15.4 Zero-Address Instruction
A stack-organized computer does not use an address field for instructions ADD and MUL.
The PUSH and POP instructions, however, need an address field to specify the operand that
communicates with the stack. The following program shows how X = (A+B) * (C+D) will be
written for a stack-organized computer (TOS stands for top-of-stack)
PUSH A TOS← A, PUSH B TOS ←B, ADD TOS ←(A + B),
PUSH C TOS ←C
PUSH D TOS ←D, ADD TOS ←(C + D) , MUL TOS ←(C + D) (A + B),
POP X M[X] ←TOS.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Immediate Mode: In this mode the operand is specified in the instruction itself. In other
words, an immediate mode instruction has an operand field rather than an address field. The
operand field contains the actual operand to be used in conjunction with the operation
specified in the instruction. Immediate mode instructions are useful for initializing registers
to a constant value.
When the address field specifies a processor register, the instruction is said to be in the
register mode.
Register Mode: In this mode the operands are in registers that reside within the CPU. The
particular register is selected from a register field in the instruction. A k-bit field can specify
any of the 2k registers.
Register Indirect Mode: In this mode the instruction specifies a register in the CPU whose
contents give the address of the operand in memory. In other words, the selected register
contains the address of the operand rather than the operand itself. Before using a register
indirect mode instruction, the programmer must ensure that the memory address of the
operand is placed in the processor register with a previous instruction. A reference to the
register is then equivalent to specifying a memory address. The advantage of the register
indirect mode instruction is that the address field of the instruction uses fewer bits to select a
register than would have been required to specify a memory address directly.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
3.9 Registers
 A register is a group of flip-flops with each flip- flop capable of storing one bit of
information.
 A register is a digital circuit used within the CPU to store one or more bits of data.
 An n-bit register has a group of n flip-flops and is capable of storing n bits of binary
information.
 In addition to Flip-Flops, it may have combinational gates that perform certain data
processing.
 Two basic types of registers are commonly used: parallel registers and shift registers.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.2.1 Connection of RAM and CPU
Data transfer between the main memory and the CPU register takes place through two
registers namely MAR (memory address register) and MDR (memory data register). If MAR
is k bits long and MDR is n bits long, the main memory unit can contain up to 2k addressable
locations.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The simplest way to organize a computer is to have one processor register and an instruction
code format with two parts. The first part of instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed and the second specifies an address. The memory address tells the control where
to find an operand in memory. This operand is read from memory and used as the data to be
operated on together with the data stored in processor register. Instructions are stored in one
section of memory and data in another. The operation is performed with memory operands
and the content of AC. Figure 5-1 below depicts this type of organization.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The control unit of a computer is designed to go through an instruction cycle that is divided
into three major phases. 1. Fetch the instruction from memory 2. Decode the instruction 3.
Execute the instruction
There is one register in the computer called the program counter (PC) that keeps track of the
instructions in the program stored in memory. PC holds the address of the instruction to be
executed next and incremented each time an instruction is fetched from memory. The
decoding done in step 2, determines the operation to be performed, the addressing mode of
the instruction, and the location of the operand.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
An Instruction Code is a group of bits that instructs the computer to perform a specific
operation. It is usually divided into parts, each having its own particular interpretation. The
most basic part of an instruction code is its operation part. The operation code of an
instruction is a group of bits that defines such operations as Add, Subtract, Multiply, Shift
and Complement. The operation part of an instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed. This operation must be performed on some data stored in processor registers or
in memory. An instruction must specify not only the operation but also the registers or the
memory words where the operands are to be found.

answer.explanation: Cache performance is explicitly measured by hit ratio, hits/(hits+misses), in PDF p.85. A hit means the requested word is found in cache (p.84), making this a direct measure of cache availability of requested data.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
• The performance of cache memory is frequently measured in terms of a quantity called hit
ratio
Hit ratio = hit / (hit+miss)
• The basic characteristic of cache memory is its fast access time
• Therefore, very little or no time must be wasted when searching the words in the cache
• The transformation of data from main memory to cache memory is referred to as a mapping

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.3 Cache Memory
Cache memory is a small, high-speed RAM buffer located between the CPU and main
memory.
Cache memory holds a copy of the instructions (instruction cache) or data (operand or data
cache) currently being used by the CPU.
The main purpose of a cache is to accelerate your computer while keeping the price of the
computer low.
• The cache is the fastest component in the memory hierarchy and approaches the speed of
CPU component
• When CPU needs to access memory, the cache is examined
• If the word is found in the cache, it is read from the fast memory
• If the word addressed by the CPU is not found in the cache, the main memory is accessed
to read the word
• When the CPU refers to memory and finds the word in cache, it is said to produce a hit
• Otherwise, it is a miss

Binary information in digital computers represented by physical quantities called signal.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module

4.2 Bus and Memory Transfers
A typical computer has many registers, and paths must be provided to transfer information
from one register to another. An efficient way for transferring information between registers

of common lines, one for each bit of a register. Control signals determine which register the

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Computer architecture: refers to those attributes of a system visible to a programmer or,
put another way, those attributes that have a direct impact on the logical execution of a
program. Examples of architectural attributes include the instruction set, the number of bits
used to represent various data types (e.g., numbers, characters), I/O mechanisms, and
techniques for addressing memory.

the architectural specifications. Organizational attributes include those hardware details
transparent to the programmer, such as control signals; interfaces between the computer and
peripherals; and the memory technology used.

module_refs.quote:
The control unit of a computer is designed to go through an instruction cycle that is divided
into three major phases. 1. Fetch the instruction from memory 2. Decode the instruction 3.
Execute the instruction
There is one register in the computer called the program counter (PC) that keeps track of the
instructions in the program stored in memory. PC holds the address of the instruction to be

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
I. Fetch the instruction
Initially, the program counter PC is loaded with the address of the first instruction in the
program and SC is cleared to 0, providing a decoded timing signal T0. After each clock
pulse, SC is incremented by one, so that the timing signals go through a sequence T0, T1, T2
and so on. Since the address lines of the memory unit are hardwired to AR, address of the
instruction to be fetched must first be placed in AR. Thus the first register transfer in an
instruction cycle should be transferring the content of PC (address of the instruction to be
brought in for execution) to AR
T0: AR ← PC
Bus selects PC, LD(AR) = 1. Next the current instruction is brought from memory into IR
and PC is incremented
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. Bus selects RAM, Memory read is set, LD(IR) = 1,
INR(PC) = 1
II. Decode the instruction
T2: D0, ... , D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)
Therefore, micro-operations for the fetch and decode phases can be specified by the
following register transfer statements.
T0: AR ← PC
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2: D0, …, D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Computer instructions are usually stored in consecutive memory locations and executed
sequentially one at a time. The control reads an instruction from specific address in memory
and executes it. It then continues by reading the next instruction in sequence and executes it
and so on. This type of instruction sequencing needs a counter to calculate the address of the
next instruction after execution of the current instruction is completed. It is also necessary to
provide a register in a control unit for storing the instruction code after it is read from the
memory. The data register (DR) holds the operand read from memory. The accumulator (AC)
register is a general purpose processing register. The instructions read from memory are
placed in instruction register (IR). The temporary register (TR) is used for holding temporary
data during the processing.

answer.explanation: The module enumerates four I/O command kinds: control, test, read and write (PDF pp.104–105). “Status command” is interpreted as the test/status-query kind, and “output data” as write. “Issue” is an action performed by CPU, not one of the four command kinds.

choices.label: B

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
7.6 I/O commands
To execute an I/O related instruction, the CPU issues an address, specifying the particular
I/O module and external device and an I/O command. Four types of I/O commands can
be received by the I/O module when it is addressed by the CPU. They are
 A control command: is used to activate a peripheral and tell what to do. Example: a

Wide variety of peripherals and delivering different amounts of data per second Work at
different speeds Send/receive data in different formats all slower than CPU and RAM. Hence

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
5.11. Central Processing Unit.
The part of the computer that performs the bulk of data processing operations is called the
Central processing unit and is referred to as the CPU. The CPU is made up of three major
parts The register set stores intermediate data used during the execution of the instructions.
The Arithmetic and Logic unit (ALU) performs the required micro-operations for executing
the instructions. The control unit supervises the transfer of information among the registers
and instructs the arithmetic and logic units as to which operation to perform. The CPU
performs a variety of functions dictated by the type of instructions that are incorporated in the
computer. Computer architecture is sometimes defined as the computer structure and
behavior as seen by the programmer that uses machine language instructions. This includes
the instruction formats, addressing modes, the instruction sets and the general organizations
of the CPU registers

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Computer architecture: refers to those attributes of a system visible to a programmer or,
put another way, those attributes that have a direct impact on the logical execution of a
program. Examples of architectural attributes include the instruction set, the number of bits
used to represent various data types (e.g., numbers, characters), I/O mechanisms, and
techniques for addressing memory.
Computer organization refers to the operational units and their interconnections that realize
the architectural specifications. Organizational attributes include those hardware details
transparent to the programmer, such as control signals; interfaces between the computer and
peripherals; and the memory technology used.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The input/output subsystem of a computer, referred to as I/O, provides an efficient mode of
communication between the central system and the outside environment. Programs and data
must be entered into computer memory for processing and results obtained from
computations must be recorded or displayed for users. A computer serves no useful purpose
without the ability to receive information from an outside source and to transmit results in a
meaningful form. I/O operations are accomplished through a wide assortment of external
devices that provide a means of exchanging data between the external environment and the
computer. An external device attaches to the computer by a link to an I/O module. The link is
used to exchange control, status, and data between the I/O module and the external device.
An external device connected to an I/O module also called Interface is often referred to as a
peripheral device or simply a peripheral.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
7.3 Classification of External devices
External devices broadly can be classified into three categories:
Human readable: suitable for communicating with the computer user. Examples: Screen,
keyboard, video display terminals (VDT) and printers.
Machine readable: suitable for communicating with equipment. Examples: magnetic disk &
tapes systems, Monitoring and control, sensors and actuators which are used in robotics.
Communication: These devices allow a computer to exchange data with remote devices,
which may be machine readable or human readable. Examples: Modem, Network Interface
Card (NIC)

6.4 Secondary memory
Devises that provides backup storage are called an Auxiliary memory (Secondary memory)
 It stores information that is not necessarily in current use.
 It is slower and having higher capacity than primary memory.
 This kind of memory is large, slow and inexpensive.
 It is non-volatile storage media i.e. the contents are not erased when the power is
switched off.
 Magnetic disk, Magnetic tape and optical disk are the examples of secondary storage.

A computer system is equipped with a hierarchy of memory subsystems. There are several
memory types with very different physical properties. The important characteristics of
memory devices are cost per bit, access time, data transfer rate, alterability and compatibility
with processor technologies. Figure shows the hierarchy of memory in a typical memory
with a trend in access time, amount of storage, and cost per byte.
Figure 6.1 memory hierarchy

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
In the programming examples of the previous chapter, we have shown that memory locations
are needed for storing pointers, counters, return addresses, temporary results and partial
product during multiplication. Having to refer to memory locations for such applications is
time consuming because memory access is the most time consuming operation in a computer.
It is more convenient and more efficient to store these intermediate values in processor
register. When a large number of registers are included in the CPU, It is most efficient to
connect them through a common bus system. The registers communicate with each other not
only for direct data transfers, but also while performing various micro operations.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.3 Cache Memory
Cache memory is a small, high-speed RAM buffer located between the CPU and main
memory.
Cache memory holds a copy of the instructions (instruction cache) or data (operand or data
cache) currently being used by the CPU.
The main purpose of a cache is to accelerate your computer while keeping the price of the
computer low.
• The cache is the fastest component in the memory hierarchy and approaches the speed of
CPU component
• When CPU needs to access memory, the cache is examined
• If the word is found in the cache, it is read from the fast memory
• If the word addressed by the CPU is not found in the cache, the main memory is accessed
to read the word
• When the CPU refers to memory and finds the word in cache, it is said to produce a hit
• Otherwise, it is a miss

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
An Instruction Code is a group of bits that instructs the computer to perform a specific
operation. It is usually divided into parts, each having its own particular interpretation. The
most basic part of an instruction code is its operation part. The operation code of an
instruction is a group of bits that defines such operations as Add, Subtract, Multiply, Shift
and Complement. The operation part of an instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed. This operation must be performed on some data stored in processor registers or
in memory. An instruction must specify not only the operation but also the registers or the
memory words where the operands are to be found.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The control unit of a computer is designed to go through an instruction cycle that is divided
into three major phases. 1. Fetch the instruction from memory 2. Decode the instruction 3.
Execute the instruction
There is one register in the computer called the program counter (PC) that keeps track of the
instructions in the program stored in memory. PC holds the address of the instruction to be
executed next and incremented each time an instruction is fetched from memory. The
decoding done in step 2, determines the operation to be performed, the addressing mode of
the instruction, and the location of the operand.

the I/O module. The CPU executes a program that gives it direct control of the I/O

 I/O module sets status bits
 CPU checks status bits periodically
 I/O module does not inform CPU directly
 I/O module does not interrupt CPU

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Programmed I/O :With Programmed I/O, data are exchanged between the CPU and
the I/O module. The CPU executes a program that gives it direct control of the I/O
operation, including sensing device status, sending a read or write command and
transferring data. When CPU issues a command to I/O module, it must wait until I/O
operation is complete. If the CPU is faster than I/O module, there is wastage of CPU
time. The I/O module does not take any further action to alert CPU. That is it doesn’t
interrupt CPU. Hence it is the responsibility of the CPU to periodically check the
status of the I/O module until it finds that the operation is complete. The sequences of
actions that take place with programmed I/O are:
 CPU requests I/O operation
 I/O module performs operation
 I/O module sets status bits
 CPU checks status bits periodically
 I/O module does not inform CPU directly
 I/O module does not interrupt CPU

The internal operation in digital system is synchronized by means of clock pulse supplied by

register.in such cases the two units are said to be asynchronous to each other. This approach
is widely used in most computers systems.
