module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Instruction Pipeline:
Pipeline processing can occur not only in the data stream but also in the instruction
stream as well. An instruction pipeline reads consecutive instructions from memory
while previous instructions are being executed in other segments. Whenever there is
space in the buffer, the control unit initiates the next instruction fetch phase. The
following steps are needed to process each instruction:
1. Fetch the instruction from memory
2. Decode the instruction
3. Calculate the effective address
4. Fetch the operands from memory
5. Execute the instruction
6. Store the result in the proper place

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.3 Cache Memory
Cache memory is a small, high-speed RAM buffer located between the CPU and main
memory.
Cache memory holds a copy of the instructions (instruction cache) or data (operand or data
cache) currently being used by the CPU.
The main purpose of a cache is to accelerate your computer while keeping the price of the
computer low.
• The cache is the fastest component in the memory hierarchy and approaches the speed of
CPU component
• When CPU needs to access memory, the cache is examined
• If the word is found in the cache, it is read from the fast memory
• If the word addressed by the CPU is not found in the cache, the main memory is accessed
to read the word
• When the CPU refers to memory and finds the word in cache, it is said to produce a hit
• Otherwise, it is a miss

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Computer instructions are usually stored in consecutive memory locations and executed
sequentially one at a time. The control reads an instruction from specific address in memory
and executes it. It then continues by reading the next instruction in sequence and executes it
and so on. This type of instruction sequencing needs a counter to calculate the address of the
next instruction after execution of the current instruction is completed. It is also necessary to
provide a register in a control unit for storing the instruction code after it is read from the
memory. The data register (DR) holds the operand read from memory. The accumulator (AC)
register is a general purpose processing register. The instructions read from memory are
placed in instruction register (IR). The temporary register (TR) is used for holding temporary
data during the processing.

6.3 Cache Memory
Cache memory is a small, high-speed RAM buffer located between the CPU and main
memory.
Cache memory holds a copy of the instructions (instruction cache) or data (operand or data
cache) currently being used by the CPU.
The main purpose of a cache is to accelerate your computer while keeping the price of the
computer low.
• The cache is the fastest component in the memory hierarchy and approaches the speed of
CPU component
• When CPU needs to access memory, the cache is examined
• If the word is found in the cache, it is read from the fast memory
• If the word addressed by the CPU is not found in the cache, the main memory is accessed
to read the word
• When the CPU refers to memory and finds the word in cache, it is said to produce a hit
• Otherwise, it is a miss

module_refs.quote:
The control unit that operates the CPU bus system directs the information flow through the
register and ALU by selecting the various components in the system. For example, to perform
the operation
R1 R2 + R3, the control must provide binary selection variables to the following selector
inputs:
1. MUX A selector (SELA): to place the content of R2 into bus A.
2. MUX selector (SELB): to place the content of R3 into bus B.
3. ALU operation selector (OPR): to provide the arithmetic add A +B.
4. Decoder destination selector (SELD): to transfer the content of output bus in to R1.
The four control selection variables are generated in the control unit and must be available at
the beginning of a clock cycle. The data from the two source registers propagates through the
gates in the multiplexers and the ALU, to the output bus, and into the inputs of the destination
register, all during the clock cycle interval. Then, when the next clock transition occurs, the
binary information from the output bus is transferred into R1. To achieve a fast response

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
I. Fetch the instruction
Initially, the program counter PC is loaded with the address of the first instruction in the
program and SC is cleared to 0, providing a decoded timing signal T0. After each clock
pulse, SC is incremented by one, so that the timing signals go through a sequence T0, T1, T2
and so on. Since the address lines of the memory unit are hardwired to AR, address of the
instruction to be fetched must first be placed in AR. Thus the first register transfer in an
instruction cycle should be transferring the content of PC (address of the instruction to be
brought in for execution) to AR
T0: AR ← PC
Bus selects PC, LD(AR) = 1. Next the current instruction is brought from memory into IR
and PC is incremented
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. Bus selects RAM, Memory read is set, LD(IR) = 1,
INR(PC) = 1
II. Decode the instruction
T2: D0, ... , D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)
Therefore, micro-operations for the fetch and decode phases can be specified by the
following register transfer statements.
T0: AR ← PC
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2: D0, …, D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)

module_refs.quote:
Instruction Pipeline:
Pipeline processing can occur not only in the data stream but also in the instruction
stream as well. An instruction pipeline reads consecutive instructions from memory
while previous instructions are being executed in other segments. Whenever there is
space in the buffer, the control unit initiates the next instruction fetch phase. The
following steps are needed to process each instruction:
1. Fetch the instruction from memory
2. Decode the instruction
3. Calculate the effective address
4. Fetch the operands from memory
5. Execute the instruction
6. Store the result in the proper place

module_refs.quote:
The control unit of a computer is designed to go through an instruction cycle that is divided
into three major phases. 1. Fetch the instruction from memory 2. Decode the instruction 3.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
A RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) processor pipeline operates in much the same
way, although the stages in the pipeline are different. While different processors have
different numbers of steps, they have basically variations of these five steps:
1. fetch instructions from memory
2. read registers and decode the instruction
3. execute the instruction or calculate an address
4. access an operand in data memory
5. write the result into a register
The length of the pipeline is dependent on the length of the longest step. Because RISC
instructions are simpler than those used in pre-RISC processors (now called CISC, or
Complex Instruction Set Computer), they are more conducive to pipelining. While CISC
instructions varied in length, RISC instructions are all the same length and can be fetched in a
single operation. Ideally, each of the stages in a RISC processor pipeline should take 1 clock
cycle so that the processor finishes an instruction each clock cycle and averages one cycle per
instruction (CPI). Among the characteristics attributed to RISC is its ability to use an efficient
instruction pipeline.

module_refs.quote:
I. Fetch the instruction
Initially, the program counter PC is loaded with the address of the first instruction in the
program and SC is cleared to 0, providing a decoded timing signal T0. After each clock

T2: D0, ... , D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)

6.3 Cache Memory
Cache memory is a small, high-speed RAM buffer located between the CPU and main
memory.
Cache memory holds a copy of the instructions (instruction cache) or data (operand or data
cache) currently being used by the CPU.
The main purpose of a cache is to accelerate your computer while keeping the price of the
computer low.
• The cache is the fastest component in the memory hierarchy and approaches the speed of
CPU component

module_refs.quote:
Computer instructions are usually stored in consecutive memory locations and executed
sequentially one at a time. The control reads an instruction from specific address in memory
and executes it. It then continues by reading the next instruction in sequence and executes it
and so on. This type of instruction sequencing needs a counter to calculate the address of the
next instruction after execution of the current instruction is completed. It is also necessary to
provide a register in a control unit for storing the instruction code after it is read from the
memory. The data register (DR) holds the operand read from memory. The accumulator (AC)
register is a general purpose processing register. The instructions read from memory are
placed in instruction register (IR). The temporary register (TR) is used for holding temporary
data during the processing.

binary information from the output bus is transferred into R1. To achieve a fast response

options.text: It holds the next instruction reference

questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 232

answer.text: It determines the operation to be done
answer.explanation: The stated field widths sum to 16 bits: 4+6+6. Their widths do not change the opcode’s purpose: operation selection (PDF p.47). Operand reference fields identify source/destination values or locations; PC tracks sequence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Destination reference is an operand/address field, not the opcode (p.47).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Operation selection is the explicit opcode definition (p.47).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Source reference belongs to the operand/address fields (p.47).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Next instruction is tracked by PC (p.70), not the opcode.

evidence.quote: An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation.
A 4-bit opcode permits at most 16 encodings, not necessarily 16 implemented instructions.
A 6-bit operand-reference field has 64 encodings; what they designate depends on the machine.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
An Instruction Code is a group of bits that instructs the computer to perform a specific
operation. It is usually divided into parts, each having its own particular interpretation. The
most basic part of an instruction code is its operation part. The operation code of an
instruction is a group of bits that defines such operations as Add, Subtract, Multiply, Shift
and Complement. The operation part of an instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed. This operation must be performed on some data stored in processor registers or
in memory. An instruction must specify not only the operation but also the registers or the
memory words where the operands are to be found.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The control unit of a computer is designed to go through an instruction cycle that is divided
into three major phases. 1. Fetch the instruction from memory 2. Decode the instruction 3.
Execute the instruction
There is one register in the computer called the program counter (PC) that keeps track of the
instructions in the program stored in memory. PC holds the address of the instruction to be
executed next and incremented each time an instruction is fetched from memory. The
decoding done in step 2, determines the operation to be performed, the addressing mode of
the instruction, and the location of the operand.

questions.stem:
Which performance metric can be used to measure the time taken to perform a read or write
operation?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 234

answer.explanation: Access time is the elapsed time from initiation to completion of a memory operation (PDF p.83). Memory cycle time is the minimum separation of successive operations. This distinguishes one read/write duration from transfer throughput or instruction fetching.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transfer rate measures an amount per unit time; it is not the single-operation interval defined on p.83.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cycle time measures spacing of successive operations, not the requested initiation-to-completion duration (p.83).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fetching is one instruction-cycle task, not the general read/write performance metric (p.55).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Access time is exactly the operation-duration definition (p.83).

evidence.quote: Access time measures latency of a read/write; cycle time is the minimum interval before another operation and may include recovery.
Transfer rate measures data per time, not individual-request delay.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The time that elapses between the initiation of an operation and completion of that operation
is called memory access time. The minimum time delay between two successive memory
operations is called memory cycle time. The cycle time is usually slightly lower than the
access time.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.1 Memory Hierarchy:
A computer system is equipped with a hierarchy of memory subsystems. There are several
memory types with very different physical properties. The important characteristics of
memory devices are cost per bit, access time, data transfer rate, alterability and compatibility
with processor technologies. Figure shows the hierarchy of memory in a typical memory
with a trend in access time, amount of storage, and cost per byte.
Figure 6.1 memory hierarchy
 Design constraints: How much? How fast? How expensive?
 Faster access time, greater cost per bit
 Greater capacity, smaller cost per bit,
 Greater capacity, slower access time.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
I. Fetch the instruction
Initially, the program counter PC is loaded with the address of the first instruction in the
program and SC is cleared to 0, providing a decoded timing signal T0. After each clock
pulse, SC is incremented by one, so that the timing signals go through a sequence T0, T1, T2
and so on. Since the address lines of the memory unit are hardwired to AR, address of the
instruction to be fetched must first be placed in AR. Thus the first register transfer in an
instruction cycle should be transferring the content of PC (address of the instruction to be
brought in for execution) to AR
T0: AR ← PC
Bus selects PC, LD(AR) = 1. Next the current instruction is brought from memory into IR
and PC is incremented
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. Bus selects RAM, Memory read is set, LD(IR) = 1,
INR(PC) = 1
II. Decode the instruction
T2: D0, ... , D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)
Therefore, micro-operations for the fetch and decode phases can be specified by the
following register transfer statements.
T0: AR ← PC
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2: D0, …, D7 ← Decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)

questions.stem: Under the textbook access-method taxonomy, how is magnetic-disk block access classified when requests identify blocks but mechanical positioning introduces delay?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 235

answer.explanation: The stated textbook taxonomy calls magnetic disk access direct: a request identifies an addressed block, but positioning creates access delay. RAM is classified as random access with broadly address-independent timing, while tape is sequential and associative access matches content. Informal usage may call disks random-access devices too, but the revised question explicitly chooses the textbook classification convention rather than treating the labels as universally exclusive.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Associative access matches by content rather than addressed disk blocks.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Tape-like sequential access is not the disk’s required access pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Random is the RAM category in the explicitly stated textbook taxonomy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct is the disk category in that taxonomy.

evidence.quote: In textbook access taxonomy, tape is sequential, disk is direct access with positioning delay, RAM is random access with broadly address-independent timing, and associative access matches content.
“Random-access disk” is also common informal usage; specify the taxonomy when comparing direct and random access.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.4.1 Magnetic Disk
 Magnetic disks are the foundation of external memory on virtually all computer
systems.
 A disk is a circular platter constructed of nonmagnetic material called the substrate
coated with a magnetisable material.
 More suitable than magnetic tapes for a wider range of applications such as
supporting direct access of data
 It is a thin, circular plate made of metal & plastic, which is coated with iron-oxide.
 We can randomly access the data.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.4.2 Magnetic Tape
 Magnetic Tape is a plastic ribbon which is usually ½ inch or ¼ inch wide & 50 to
2400 feet long.
 It is coated with iron-oxide material.
 It is similar to the tape of audio cassettes of tape recorders. Data is stored as binary
digits.
 Data is accessed sequentially so searching becomes difficult.
 Tape systems use the same reading and recording techniques as disk systems..
 Magnetic tape was the first kind of secondary memory.It is still widely used as the
lowest-cost, slowest-speed member of the memory hierarchy.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Associative Mapping
 An associative mapping uses an associative memory.
 This memory is being accessed using its contents.
 Associative memory is expensive compared to RAM
 Each line of cache memory will accommodate the address (main memory) and the
contents of that address from the main memory.
 That is why this memory is also called Content Addressable Memory (CAM). It
allows each block of main memory to be stored in the cache.
A CPU address of 15 bits is places in the argument register and the associative memory us
searched for a matching address
• If the address is found, the corresponding 12bits data is read and sent to the CPU
• If not, the main memory is accessed for the word
If the cache is full, an address-data pair must be displaced to make room for a pair that is
needed and not presently in the cache

questions.stem: Which statement reverses the broad integration trend described for computer evolution?
questions.hint: Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 236

answer.explanation: The note describes a broad trend toward smaller individual components while density, capacity and processor performance increase. Increasing component size reverses that stated trend. The other alternatives describe growth in performance, integration density or memory capacity and are therefore consistent with it. These are historical tendencies, not guarantees that every later product improves every measured property.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The broad trend reduces individual component dimensions, so increasing size reverses it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rising processor performance is consistent with the stated evolutionary tendency.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Increasing integration density is explicitly part of the stated integration trend.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Growing storage capacity is consistent with the stated trend even as individual component dimensions shrink.

evidence.quote: Integration generally reduced individual component dimensions while capacity, density and processor performance grew; these are trends rather than guarantees for every model.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
6.1 Memory Hierarchy:
A computer system is equipped with a hierarchy of memory subsystems. There are several
memory types with very different physical properties. The important characteristics of
memory devices are cost per bit, access time, data transfer rate, alterability and compatibility
with processor technologies. Figure shows the hierarchy of memory in a typical memory
with a trend in access time, amount of storage, and cost per byte.
Figure 6.1 memory hierarchy
 Design constraints: How much? How fast? How expensive?
 Faster access time, greater cost per bit
 Greater capacity, smaller cost per bit,
 Greater capacity, slower access time.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
RISC characteristics
• Relatively few instructions
• Relatively few addressing modes
• Memory access limited to load and store instructions
• All operations done within the register of the CPU
• Fixed length, easily decoded instruction format
• Single cycle instruction execution
• Hard-wired rather than micro-programmed control
• A relatively large number of registers in the processor
• Use overlapped register windows to speed up procedure call and return
• Efficient instruction pipeline
• Compiler support for efficient transmission high-level language programs into machine
language programs

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
5.19 CISC Instruction:
CISC refers to Complex Instruction Set Computer
CISC characteristic
• Large number of instructions – typically from 100 to 250 instructions
• Some instructions that perform specialized tasks and are used infrequently
• A large variety of addressing modes – typically from 5 to 20 different modes
• Variable length instruction formats
• Instructions that manipulate operands in memory RISC characteristics

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
3.1 Integrated Circuits
 Integrated circuit (IC) is the basic building block of digital circuits.
 An integrated circuit is a small silicon semiconductor crystal, called a chip.
 The various gates are interconnected inside the chip to form the required circuit.
 As the technology of ICs has improved, the number of gates that can be put in a single
chip has increased.
 Small-scale integration (SSI) devices contain several (usually less than 10)
independent gates in a single package.
 Medium-scale integration (MSI) devices contain approximately 10 to 200 gates in a
single package.
E.g To form decoders, adders, and registers.
 Large-scale integration (LSI) devices contain between 200 and a few thousands
gates in a single package.
Eg. processors, memory chips, and programmable modules.
 Very-large-scale integration (VLSI) devices contain thousands of gates in a single
package.
E.g large memory arrays and complex microcomputer chips.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is NOT correct about Von Neumann's architecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Data and instructions are stored separately

options.label: B
options.text: Modern computers are based on Von Neumann's architecture

options.label: D
options.text: Memory content is located by its address

questions.hint: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 237

answer.text: Separate instruction and data storage contradicts the textbook Von Neumann model.
answer.explanation: COA02 defines the textbook Von Neumann model as sharing an addressed memory system between instructions and data, with normally sequential execution unless control flow changes. Thus separate storage is the defining contradiction. The note allows modern machines to retain a unified address-space view while using split caches; ordinary execution and addressed memory remain compatible with that model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Separate instruction/data memories describe Harvard organization rather than the textbook shared-memory Von Neumann model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Modern systems can retain a unified address-space view, so this broad conventional association is compatible with the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Normally sequential instruction progression is part of the textbook model, with branches providing explicit control-flow changes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The model explicitly uses addressed memory, so locating content by address is a compatible statement.

evidence.quote: In the textbook Von Neumann model, instructions and data share an addressed memory system; the CPU normally advances sequentially unless control flow changes.
Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
The simplest way to organize a computer is to have one processor register and an instruction
code format with two parts. The first part of instruction code specifies the operation to be
performed and the second specifies an address. The memory address tells the control where
to find an operand in memory. This operand is read from memory and used as the data to be
operated on together with the data stored in processor register. Instructions are stored in one
section of memory and data in another. The operation is performed with memory operands
and the content of AC. Figure 5-1 below depicts this type of organization.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Computer instructions are usually stored in consecutive memory locations and executed
sequentially one at a time. The control reads an instruction from specific address in memory
and executes it. It then continues by reading the next instruction in sequence and executes it
and so on. This type of instruction sequencing needs a counter to calculate the address of the
next instruction after execution of the current instruction is completed. It is also necessary to
provide a register in a control unit for storing the instruction code after it is read from the
memory. The data register (DR) holds the operand read from memory. The accumulator (AC)
register is a general purpose processing register. The instructions read from memory are
placed in instruction register (IR). The temporary register (TR) is used for holding temporary
data during the processing.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Instruction Set Completeness
A computer should have a set of instructions so that the user can construct machine language
program to evaluate any function that is known to be computable. The set of instructions are
said to be complete if the computer includes a sufficient number of instructions in each of the
following categories:
1. Arithmetic, Logical and Shift Instructions.
2. Instructions for moving information to and from memory and processor registers.
3. Program control instructions together with instructions that check status conditions.
4. Input and Output instructions.

questions.stem: Which instruction type is used to test the value of a data word or status of a condition?
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 238

answer.explanation: COA19 states that TEST/CMP examine values and set condition information, often without retaining an arithmetic result. That exactly matches examining a data word or a condition status. Arithmetic/data processing is a broader computing class, data movement copies values, and branches choose control-flow targets. The named test-instruction category is therefore the direct answer among the options.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Data processing is a broader computing category; the stem specifically requests the instruction used to test values.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: TEST/CMP examine values and establish condition information, directly matching the question’s described operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Data movement copies values between locations rather than testing their contents or condition status.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Branches choose control-flow targets, often using previously established conditions rather than performing the requested test.

evidence.quote: TEST/CMP examine values and set condition information, often without retaining the arithmetic result.
Branch instructions choose a target, conditionally or unconditionally.
CALL saves a return point; RETURN restores it.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Data Manipulation
Data manipulation instructions perform operations on data and provide the computational
capabilities for the computer. The data manipulation instructions in a typical computer are
usually divided into three basic types.
1. Arithmetic instruction
2. Logical and bit manipulation
3. Shift instruction
a. Arithmetic Instruction
The four basic arithmetic operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
Most computers provide instructions for all four operations. Some small computers have only
addition and possibly subtraction instructions. The multiplication and division must then be
generated by means of software subroutines.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Direct Addressing Mode: In this mode the effective address is equal to the address part of
the instruction. The operand resides in memory and its address is given directly by the
address field of the instruction. In a branch type of instruction the address field specifies the
actual branch address.
Indirect Addressing Mode: In this mode the address field of the instruction gives the
address where the effective address is stored in memory. Control fetches the instruction from
memory and uses its address part to access memory again to read the effective address.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Data transfer instruction.
Data transfer instructions move data from place to place in the computer to another without
changing the data content. The most common transfers are between memory and processor
registers, between processor register and input or output, and between the processor registers
themselves. Table 5-5 gives lists of eight data transfer instructions used in many computers.
Accompanying each instruction is mnemonic symbol.

module_refs.title: Computer Organization and Architecture module
module_refs.quote:
Instruction Set Completeness
A computer should have a set of instructions so that the user can construct machine language
program to evaluate any function that is known to be computable. The set of instructions are
said to be complete if the computer includes a sufficient number of instructions in each of the
following categories:
1. Arithmetic, Logical and Shift Instructions.
2. Instructions for moving information to and from memory and processor registers.
3. Program control instructions together with instructions that check status conditions.
4. Input and Output instructions.

questions.stem:
What is the purpose of an opcode in a 16-bit instruction format (4-bit opcode | 6-bit operand ref 
6-bit operand ref)?

options.label: A
options.text: It holds the destination address of an operand

options.label: B
options.text: It determines the operation to be done

options.label: C
options.text: It holds the source address of an operand

options.label: D
options.text: It holds the next instruction reference

questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 232

answer.explanation: COA16 defines the opcode as specifying the operation and operand fields as locating data/registers. In the given 16-bit format, the 4-bit opcode therefore selects an operation, while the two 6-bit references identify operands under the machine’s interpretation. The bit widths are not evidence that the opcode stores a source/destination address or next-PC reference.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A destination operand reference belongs in an operand field, not in the operation-selecting opcode.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The opcode determines which operation the processor should perform for this instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A source operand reference is an operand-field role rather than the opcode’s operation role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The next-instruction reference is a control-flow/PC concern, not the general purpose of this opcode field.

evidence.quote: An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation.

questions.stem: A designer adds a PCI expansion card to a processor whose local bus uses a different transfer protocol. The two sides cannot be wired together directly. Which listed hardware category is needed to adapt transfers between the processor bus and the expansion interconnect?
questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 6

answer.explanation: The scenario requires hardware that adapts transfers between unlike bus segments, so bus bridge/controller logic is needed. PCI identifies the expansion interconnect on one side of the connection; merely naming it does not supply the adaptation to the processor bus. SCSI identifies a storage connection and Multibus another bus family. The distinction is between the interconnect being attached and the hardware that enables the attachment.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SCSI is a storage connection rather than the adapter between these unlike bus segments.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: PCI names the expansion interconnect already present in the scenario, not the adapting component.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bus bridge/controller logic adapts transfers between the unlike processor and expansion bus segments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multibus names a bus family rather than the component needed to adapt this connection.

evidence.quote: PCI is a peripheral expansion interconnect, not a disk protocol; connecting unlike bus segments requires suitable bridge/controller logic.

questions.stem: Combinational circuit differ from sequential circuit primarily because

options.label: A
options.text: Combinational circuit cannot be built using logic circuit

options.label: B
options.text:
The output of combinational circuit depends only on the present input, not on past 
output.

options.label: C
options.text: Sequential circuit have no feedback while combinational circuit do

options.label: D
options.text: The combinational circuit requires clock signal, but sequential circuit do not

questions.hint: Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 7

answer.text: Combinational output depends on present inputs rather than stored history.
answer.explanation: COA05 defines combinational output through present inputs after propagation delay, while sequential output also depends on stored state. B expresses that distinction. Combinational circuits are built from logic, not prohibited from it; the feedback statement reverses the usual state relationship. Nor do combinational circuits inherently require a clock, while clocked sequential circuits update at clock events.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Combinational circuits are logic circuits; the statement incorrectly denies their ordinary implementation basis.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Present inputs determine combinational outputs, whereas sequential circuits additionally depend on retained state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This reverses the state/feedback distinction; sequential storage can involve feedback, not its categorical absence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Combinational logic does not inherently require a clock; clock events characterize clocked sequential updates.

evidence.quote: A combinational output depends on present inputs after propagation delay.
A sequential circuit depends on stored state as well as inputs; registers, counters and flip-flops are examples.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is the first operation or step in CPU instruction cycle?
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 22

answer.explanation: COA15 begins the conceptual instruction cycle with fetch, then decode, operand acquisition, execution and any result write-back. Fetch must obtain the instruction before its opcode can be decoded and operation performed. Permitted interrupt checks are a separate stage/transition in that conceptual model, not the first ordinary instruction-processing step among these choices.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Execution follows obtaining and decoding the instruction, rather than being the cycle’s first conceptual step.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Interrupt checks/service are distinct from the first ordinary fetch step in the note’s conceptual cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Decoding requires an already fetched instruction, so it follows rather than precedes fetch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Fetching obtains the instruction and is explicitly first in the conceptual instruction-cycle sequence.

evidence.quote: A conceptual instruction cycle fetches an instruction, decodes opcode/addressing fields, obtains operands, executes, writes results where required and checks permitted interrupts.

questions.stem:
____________ is a data transfer method in computer organization and architecture that 
allows an I/O device to transfer data directly to or from memory without the involvement 
of the CPU.
questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 31

answer.explanation: COA30 says DMA lets a controller transfer a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup. The stem’s without CPU involvement must mean without CPU moving every item, not no configuration/completion involvement whatsoever. Polling and interrupt-driven I/O still require CPU transfer work; asynchronous transfer describes timing coordination rather than this block-moving mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Asynchronous transfer describes coordination/timing rather than specifically controller-managed movement directly between device and memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DMA transfers the block through a controller after CPU setup, avoiding per-item CPU copying.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interrupt-driven handlers still consume CPU time to service and move device data in this comparison.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Programmed I/O repeatedly checks status and has the CPU move each item rather than using DMA.

evidence.quote: DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.
Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.

questions.stem: Which logic gate produces output 1 only when ALL inputs are 1?
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 1

answer.explanation: COA03 states that AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1. This is exactly the condition in the stem. OR needs any high input, NAND complements AND, and two-input XOR is high when inputs differ. Thus none of the other truth functions has the specified all-high-only output rule.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: OR becomes high when any input is high, so it does not require all inputs to be one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: AND outputs one exactly for the all-inputs-one combination required by the stem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NAND inverts AND and therefore outputs zero, not one, when all its inputs are one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Two-input XOR outputs one when inputs differ, not when both inputs are one.

evidence.quote: AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR is 1 if any input is 1.

questions.stem: The Boolean expression F = A⊕B represents which gate?
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 2

answer.explanation: The expression A⊕B is the exclusive-OR operation. COA03 defines its two-input output as 1 when the inputs differ and contrasts XNOR as agreement. NOR and NAND complement OR and AND instead. Thus XOR is the operation represented by the given symbol, with no extra circuit diagram or numeric assumption needed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: XNOR is the complement of XOR, giving one when the two inputs agree.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NOR complements OR; it is not the exclusive-OR operation denoted by the circled plus.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The circled-plus expression denotes exclusive OR, whose output is one for differing inputs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NAND complements AND rather than implementing the given exclusive-OR expression.

evidence.quote: The circled plus symbol ⊕ denotes exclusive OR.
NAND complements AND; NOR complements OR.
For two inputs XOR is 1 when inputs differ, and XNOR when they agree.

questions.stem: Which gate is called the 'universal gate' because it can implement any Boolean function?
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 3

answer.text: NAND, the only universal gate offered.
answer.explanation: COA04 explicitly states that NAND and NOR are each universal and explains constructing NOT by tying inputs together, then building AND/OR combinations. Of those two universal families, only NAND is offered. AND and OR alone cannot provide inversion under this rule, and XOR is not identified as a universal family. Thus the correct offered gate is NAND.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: AND alone is not the universal family described; it does not supply the required inversion construction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: OR alone is not the universal family described and cannot generate the stated NOT construction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NAND is explicitly universal and can be combined to construct NOT, AND and OR.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: XOR is not the NAND/NOR universal family; tied inputs produce zero rather than inversion.

evidence.quote: NAND and NOR are each universal: feeding the same input to both inputs constructs NOT; combine complemented gates to construct AND or OR.

questions.stem: For a NOR gate with inputs A=1, B=0, the output F is:
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 4

answer.explanation: COA03 defines OR as high when any input is high and NOR as its complement. At A=1, B=0, the OR value is 1, so NOR produces 0. The input combination is completely specified in ordinary Boolean logic; it is neither undefined nor dependent on an unspecified analog voltage model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: OR of 1 and 0 is 1; complementing that for NOR yields zero.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One is the OR result before inversion, not the NOR output for these inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The Boolean NOR truth table fully defines this ordinary input combination.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The stem supplies Boolean input values, so no additional voltage threshold assumption is required.

evidence.quote: AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR is 1 if any input is 1.
NAND complements AND; NOR complements OR.

questions.stem: De Morgan's theorem states that NOT(A·B) equals:
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 5

answer.explanation: COA04 gives (AB)'=A'+B'. Complementing a product changes AND to OR and complements each operand. B matches that exact transformation. A instead gives the complement of A+B, C omits the operand complements, and D leaves the complement attached to a sum, which represents NOR rather than the requested NAND function.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The product of complements equals NOT(A+B), rather than the complement of the original product.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Complement each operand and change AND to OR, exactly as De Morgan’s product rule states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A+B omits both required complements and is not generally equal to NOT(A·B).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NOT(A+B) is NOR and differs from NOT(A·B), for example when only one input is high.

evidence.quote: De Morgan gives (AB)'=A'+B' and (A+B)'=A'B'.

questions.stem: In Boolean algebra, the expression A + A' (A OR NOT A) always equals:
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 6

answer.explanation: COA04 explicitly lists A+A'=1. If A is 0 then A' is 1, and if A is 1 then A' is 0; either way their Boolean OR is 1. Neither A nor A' remains fixed across both assignments, and zero is the product-of-complements result rather than their sum.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Zero is A AND NOT A; the given operation is OR, so one input is always high.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A can be zero while the expression remains one, so the identity is not simply A.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A bit OR its complement is always one for both possible assignments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A complement can be zero while the full expression is one, so it is not the constant result.

evidence.quote: Useful identities are A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A, AA=A, A+A'=1, AA'=0, A+AB=A and A(A+B)=A.

questions.stem: How many rows are in the truth table for a Boolean function with 4 input variables?
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 7

answer.explanation: COA03 gives 2^n rows for n binary inputs. For four independent variables, each has two assignments, so the total combinations are 2×2×2×2=16. The options 8 and 32 correspond to three and five binary variables respectively; 12 does not enumerate all four-variable combinations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eight is 2^3, the number of assignments for three inputs rather than four.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Twelve omits four of the sixteen possible combinations of four independent binary inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Four independent binary inputs yield 2^4=16 distinct truth-table rows.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is 2^5 and would require five independent binary input variables.

evidence.quote: With n binary inputs, enumerate 2^n truth-table rows.

questions.stem: For the Boolean function F=x+y'z with x=0,y=1,z=1, which options evaluate to the same Boolean value as F under that assignment? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 8

answer.explanation: Complement first: y is one, so y-prime is zero. The product y-prime AND z is therefore zero, and OR with x, also zero, leaves F equal to zero. Both the literal zero option and the expression x evaluate to that result under the stated assignment. The literal one and z both evaluate to one. The multiple-selection wording preserves the actual option values rather than arbitrarily rejecting an equivalent expression.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The literal zero equals the computed function value.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One differs from the computed zero.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: x is assigned zero and therefore equals the function value.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: z is assigned one and differs from the function value.

evidence.quote: Evaluate complements, products and then sums.
A plus sign means Boolean OR, not integer addition.
Useful identities are A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A, AA=A, A+A'=1, AA'=0, A+AB=A and A(A+B)=A.

questions.stem: Which characteristic best describes a flip-flop?

options.label: B
options.text: A bistable multivibrator that stores one bit

questions.hint: Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 9

answer.explanation: COA05 says a flip-flop stores one bit while powered and classifies flip-flops as sequential circuits with stored state. B is the option describing that storage element. A combinational circuit lacks stored logical state; a four-bit counter requires a multi-bit state structure, and an arithmetic unit computes rather than defining this one-bit storage component.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A combinational circuit has no stored logical state, whereas a flip-flop retains a bit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bistable one-bit storage matches the powered state-retention role of a flip-flop.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One flip-flop stores one bit; a four-bit counter requires a multi-bit state organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An arithmetic unit computes values rather than defining the one-bit sequential storage element.

evidence.quote: A flip-flop is bistable: it has two stable states representing 0 and 1.
Multiple flip-flops are required to represent a multi-bit counter state.
A combinational output depends on present inputs after propagation delay.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a flip-flop from a simple logic gate in terms of memory?

options.label: B
options.text: Flip-flops retain state even after inputs change

questions.hint: Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 10

answer.text: Flip-flops retain stored state during powered operation.
answer.explanation: COA05 distinguishes sequential state from combinational outputs determined by present inputs. A flip-flop can retain its bit when inputs change without a qualifying update, giving the memory distinction in B. This does not imply nonvolatile retention after power-off. Power, speed and AC-supply claims are neither the defining property nor guarantees established here.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Power consumption is implementation-dependent and does not define whether a circuit has logical memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Stored state persists between valid updates while powered, unlike a purely present-input combinational gate.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Speed is not the defining memory distinction and is not guaranteed by the flip-flop label.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note specifies powered storage, not a requirement for an AC rather than another supply.

evidence.quote: A flip-flop stores one bit while powered.
State retention during operation does not mean nonvolatile storage.

questions.stem: What is the decimal equivalent of binary number 1011?
questions.hint: Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 11

answer.explanation: Using COA08’s base-position rule, 1011₂ has weights 8, 4, 2 and 1. Its high bits contribute 8+2+1=11, while the 4-place is zero. The note’s worked example confirms the same sum. Nine, ten and thirteen correspond to different low-order bit patterns, not the supplied 1011.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Nine equals 8+1, corresponding to 1001₂ and omitting the given two-place bit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ten equals 8+2, corresponding to 1010₂ and omitting the given one-place bit.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The set bit positions contribute 8+2+1=11 in decimal.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirteen equals 8+4+1, corresponding to 1101₂ rather than the supplied 1011₂.

evidence.quote: In base b, a digit at position i has value digit×b^i.
Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.

questions.stem: In hexadecimal, what does the letter 'F' represent in decimal?
questions.hint: Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 12

answer.explanation: COA08 defines hexadecimal digits as 0–9,A–F and explicitly gives F=15. These sixteen symbols represent values zero through fifteen, so sixteen itself requires the two-digit hexadecimal representation 10. Fourteen is E, and ten is A, leaving fifteen as the only value of the single digit F.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fourteen corresponds to the preceding hexadecimal digit E, not the final digit F.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note explicitly assigns decimal value fifteen to the hexadecimal digit F.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sixteen requires hexadecimal 10; it is outside the value range of a single hexadecimal digit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ten corresponds to hexadecimal A rather than the later digit F.

evidence.quote: Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.

questions.stem: The octal number system uses a base of:
questions.hint: Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 13

answer.explanation: COA08 gives octal digits 0–7: eight possible digit values, so octal has base eight. Binary has two digits, decimal ten and hexadecimal sixteen. Place weights in octal are therefore powers of eight, not powers of two, ten or sixteen, even though octal digits can be grouped with three binary bits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Base two is binary; octal allows eight digit values rather than only zero and one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Octal uses digits zero through seven, giving a base of eight.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Base ten is decimal, not the eight-digit octal number system.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Base sixteen is hexadecimal, which uses the additional A–F digits absent from octal.

evidence.quote: In base b, a digit at position i has value digit×b^i.
Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.

questions.stem: Which number system is most fundamental to digital computing and why?

options.label: B
options.text: Octal, because it maps to 3 bits

options.label: C
options.text: Binary, because digital circuits have two states (on/off)

questions.hint: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 14

answer.text: Binary matches the two logical states used by digital logic.
answer.explanation: COA03 defines digital gates using the two Boolean values 0 and 1, and COA08 defines binary using exactly those two digits. That direct correspondence explains why binary is fundamental to the digital representation described here. Octal and hexadecimal group binary bits for convenience, while decimal’s human familiarity does not supply the two-state circuit correspondence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Human decimal familiarity does not match the two Boolean states used here’s digital gates.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Octal groups three binary bits and is a convenient notation rather than the underlying two-state representation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Binary digits zero and one directly correspond to the two logical values used by digital circuits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hexadecimal compactly groups four binary bits; compact notation does not replace the underlying binary states.

evidence.quote: Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.
NOT complements a bit.

questions.stem: How many bits are needed to represent the hexadecimal digit F?
questions.hint: Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 15

answer.explanation: COA08 groups four binary bits for each hexadecimal digit and gives F=15. COA09’s unsigned range shows three bits reach only 7, while four bits reach 15. Therefore the minimum representation of F is four bits, 1111. Eight bits can contain the value but are not the number needed for one hexadecimal digit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two bits encode only zero through three, insufficient for hexadecimal F’s decimal value fifteen.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Three bits encode only zero through seven, so they cannot represent the value fifteen.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Four bits encode zero through fifteen; F is represented by the four-bit pattern 1111.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Eight bits could contain fifteen but exceed the minimum four bits needed for a hexadecimal digit.

evidence.quote: Group binary bits in threes for octal and fours for hexadecimal, outward from the radix point.
Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.
For n-bit unsigned values the range is 0 through 2^n−1.

questions.stem: Which listed memory categories lose their contents when power is removed? Assume ordinary SRAM/DRAM RAM and an SRAM-based processor cache. Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 16

answer.explanation: Ordinary SRAM and DRAM require power to retain their contents. RAM therefore qualifies, and the stated SRAM-based cache qualifies for the same technological reason. Cache is a hierarchy role rather than a promise of nonvolatile storage. ROM and flash retain contents without power, so they are excluded. Specifying implementation makes the volatility judgment definite while keeping both valid categories rather than forcing a RAM-only answer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ROM retains contents without power.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Flash retains contents without power.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary SRAM/DRAM RAM is volatile.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The explicitly SRAM-based cache is volatile too.

evidence.quote: SRAM uses powered bistable storage: fast and costly per bit, without periodic refresh.
DRAM stores charge and requires refresh: denser and commonly used for main memory.
Both are ordinarily volatile.
ROM and flash retain contents without power; erasable/programmed variants mean “ROM can never be modified” is too broad.

questions.stem: Cache memory is best described as:

options.label: B
options.text: Small, ultra-fast memory between CPU and RAM

questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 17

answer.text: Small, fast storage near the CPU between it and main memory.
answer.explanation: COA23 places cache above DRAM in the usual speed/cost hierarchy and says faster levels are generally smaller and more expensive per bit. It defines cache as copied memory blocks near the CPU. B captures that role. Cache is not the large slow backup layer or disk-based virtual-memory backing store; its useful speed derives from proximity/reuse, not guaranteed persistence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Large slow cheap storage describes lower hierarchy levels rather than the small fast cache layer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cache is a small fast near-CPU copy of memory blocks used to accelerate access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note defines cache for accelerated reuse, not as nonvolatile backup storage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Disk-backed virtual memory is a different address-space/backing-store mechanism from the CPU cache.

evidence.quote: A usual speed/cost-per-bit order is registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, DRAM, SSD, HDD and archival tape.
Faster levels are generally smaller and more expensive per bit.
Cache copies memory blocks near the CPU.

questions.stem: In direct memory mapping, what happens when two different main memory blocks map to the same cache slot?

options.label: B
options.text: A cache conflict occurs and one block replaces the other

questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 18

answer.text: A placement conflict: only one block can occupy that direct-mapped slot.
answer.explanation: COA25 states that two blocks with the same direct-mapped index cannot reside together. When the requested block differs from the valid block at that slot, the cache must replace the slot’s contents, producing a conflict miss. This is ordinary cache operation, not a crash or merging of block contents; direct mapping offers no alternate placement for the same index.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One direct-mapped line holds one block at a time, so the colliding blocks cannot coexist there.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The shared index causes a placement conflict; installing the requested block replaces the current one.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Conflict replacement is ordinary cache behavior and does not imply a system crash.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cache replacement preserves separate memory-block identities; it does not merge their contents into one block.

evidence.quote: Direct mapping uses line=block mod L.
Two blocks with the same direct-mapped index cannot reside together.

questions.stem: Which cache mapping technique offers the most flexibility in placing data blocks?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 19

answer.explanation: COA25 says direct mapping fixes one line, set associativity permits any way within one indexed set, and fully associative placement permits any line. Allowing every line gives the most placement flexibility for a fixed cache. The sequential-mapping option is not one of the cache placement rules defined by the supplied note.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct mapping restricts a block to a single line and therefore has the least placement freedom.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Set associativity permits several ways in one set, fewer locations than the entire fully associative cache.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fully associative placement allows any cache line, maximizing placement freedom for each block.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sequential ordering is not a placement freedom comparable to the defined direct, set-associative and fully associative cache rules.

evidence.quote: Direct mapping uses line=block mod L.
Fully associative placement permits any line.
A W-way set-associative cache has S=L/W sets and set=block mod S; any of W ways in that set may hold the block.

questions.stem: Set associative mapping is described as a compromise between:
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 20

answer.explanation: COA25 defines W-way set associativity as fixing a set by the block index while allowing any of W ways inside it. That combines direct indexing with an associative choice within the selected set, placing it between one-line direct mapping and unrestricted fully associative placement. RAM/ROM and primary/secondary are technology/hierarchy contrasts, not the two placement endpoints.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RAM and ROM describe memory types rather than the placement-policy endpoints combined by set associativity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Set indexing restricts placement like direct mapping while allowing an associative choice among the selected set’s ways.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Primary and secondary describe hierarchy roles, not the direct versus associative cache-placement alternatives.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cache and virtual memory are different mechanisms rather than the two placement extremes defining set associativity.

evidence.quote: Direct mapping uses line=block mod L.
Fully associative placement permits any line.
A W-way set-associative cache has S=L/W sets and set=block mod S; any of W ways in that set may hold the block.

questions.stem: Virtual memory primarily uses which storage device to extend the apparent memory size?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 21

answer.text: Hard disk / SSD as backing storage.
answer.explanation: COA27 says backing storage can hold nonresident pages while virtual memory provides translated protected address spaces. COA28 identifies HDDs and SSDs as persistent storage devices, matching that backing role. ROM, cache and registers are not the nonresident-page backing tier described. Apparent extension does not mean physical RAM is added or that virtual memory is only disk disguised as RAM.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ROM stores persistent firmware/data but is not the writable nonresident-page backing role described here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cache holds near-CPU copies of memory blocks rather than serving as the mass backing store.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Persistent HDD/SSD storage can hold nonresident page contents for the virtual-memory system.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Registers hold immediate execution state and cannot serve as the large backing store for nonresident pages.

evidence.quote: Virtual memory gives processes translated address spaces and protection; backing storage can hold nonresident pages.
An HDD stores magnetic patterns on tracks divided into sectors; reads/writes access addressed blocks while platters rotate.
SSDs use nonvolatile semiconductor storage without mechanical seek.

questions.stem: A valid disk-backed virtual page is currently nonresident, and the access must load its saved contents before continuing. Which condition describes the resulting page-fault case?

options.label: A
options.text: The CPU runs out of registers

options.label: B
options.text: The requested page is not in physical memory and must be loaded from disk

questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 22

answer.text: The requested page is not in physical memory and must be loaded from disk
answer.explanation: Accessing the valid but nonresident disk-backed page faults so that the system can make the page resident and continue. The stated case requires loading its saved contents. Register pressure, cache replacement and arithmetic overflow are different conditions. Other kinds of page fault need not read a disk, so the question explicitly limits itself to this nonresident disk-backed case.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Register allocation pressure is not an access to a missing or forbidden virtual page.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The described disk-backed nonresident access is a page-fault case, although not all faults require a disk read.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A full cache leads to cache replacement, not necessarily a virtual-memory page fault.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Arithmetic overflow is an instruction arithmetic condition rather than a virtual-page access event.

evidence.quote: A valid nonresident page access faults and may require loading data; invalid or forbidden accesses can also fault.
A cache miss, TLB miss and page fault are different events; not every page fault reads a disk, since zero-fill and already-resident shared pages exist.

questions.stem: Compared to RAM, a Hard Disk Drive (HDD) is:
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 23

answer.text: HDD is generally slower and nonvolatile.
answer.explanation: COA23 places DRAM above HDD in the usual speed hierarchy. COA28 says an HDD does not require continuous power to preserve stored bits, while COA24 calls ordinary SRAM/DRAM volatile. Combining the independent speed and retention rules gives slower and nonvolatile. The answer concerns the usual hierarchy comparison rather than every conceivable workload or specialized memory device.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It reverses both usual properties: HDD is slower than RAM and retains data without power.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The hierarchy places HDD below RAM in speed, and magnetic storage preserves bits without continuous power.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nonvolatility is right, but the claim that HDD is faster than RAM reverses the usual hierarchy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Slower is right, but volatile contradicts the note’s explicit HDD power-off retention statement.

evidence.quote: A usual speed/cost-per-bit order is registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, DRAM, SSD, HDD and archival tape.
Both are ordinarily volatile.
It does not need continuous power to preserve stored bits.

questions.stem: Which range matches the historical optical-disk access-time examples used in this course, rather than a universal specification for every optical drive?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 24

answer.explanation: The note identifies one hundred to three hundred milliseconds as a historical optical-access example. That range is not a universal specification: actual timing depends on the device and measurement conditions. The revised stem asks for the particular teaching range rather than an unqualified typical value for all optical disks. The remaining intervals do not match that historical example and therefore are definite distractors.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This interval does not match the historical optical-access example.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This shorter interval is not the course’s cited historical example.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the historical example range given in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This longer interval is not the course’s cited historical example.

evidence.quote: Optical access ranges such as 100–300 ms are historical examples, not universal device specifications.

questions.stem: Which storage medium accesses data sequentially rather than randomly?
questions.hint: Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 25

answer.explanation: COA28 classifies tape as sequential and suited to streaming/archives. Disk provides direct addressed-block access, while SSD provides nonmechanical persistent storage rather than a tape-style stream. The question asks the medium whose access is characteristically sequential, so magnetic tape is the supported choice. Physical streaming inside another device does not make its logical access interface tape-like.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SSD is addressed nonvolatile semiconductor storage rather than the sequential tape-access medium described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: HDD permits addressed-block direct access rather than requiring tape-like sequential record traversal.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Tape is explicitly the sequential streaming/archive medium in the note’s access taxonomy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optical disk uses addressed disk access rather than being the sequential tape medium requested.

evidence.quote: Optical media use lasers; tape is suited to sequential streaming and archives.
In textbook access taxonomy, tape is sequential, disk is direct access with positioning delay, RAM is random access with broadly address-independent timing, and associative access matches content.

questions.stem: Registers within the CPU are used primarily to:

options.label: B
options.text: Hold temporary data for immediate CPU operations

questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 26

answer.text: Hold temporary values for immediate CPU operations.
answer.explanation: COA14 distinguishes registers as explicit execution operands and assigns them fetched instructions, transferred data and operands/results. That supports the immediate temporary-storage role in B. Registers are small execution state rather than permanent bulk data storage. Some registers participate in I/O or translation, but those specialized uses do not replace the primary execution-storage role asked here.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Registers are small temporary execution storage rather than permanent bulk storage for large datasets.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Registers hold operands, instruction state and intermediate results used directly by current CPU operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Some registers support I/O, but general I/O communication is not their primary execution-storage purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Translation can use specialized state, but managing virtual pages is not the primary role of CPU registers generally.

evidence.quote: IR holds the fetched instruction; MAR holds an address used for the current memory access; MDR holds transferred data.
The accumulator holds operands/results, SP tracks the stack, and status flags report conditions.
Registers and cache both store temporary information, but registers are explicit execution operands and cache holds copies of memory blocks.

questions.stem: The address bus in a computer system is responsible for:

options.label: B
options.text: Specifying the memory location the CPU wants to access

questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 27

answer.explanation: COA12 says address signals select a location, data signals carry values and control signals coordinate read/write and timing. Therefore B directly matches the address bus. Actual payload data belongs to the data bus, while timing and operation commands belong to control signaling. The distinction does not depend on address width or the value being transferred.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actual payload values travel on the data bus rather than the address signals selecting a location.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The address bus identifies the memory location selected for the CPU’s access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Timing belongs to control signaling, not the location-selection role of address signals.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Read/write and other operation commands belong to control signaling rather than the address bus.

evidence.quote: Address signals select a location; data signals carry values; control signals coordinate read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements.

questions.stem: A CPU exposes 32 address bits and uses byte-addressable memory with no additional address-extension mechanism. What maximum byte capacity can it address? Use GB here to mean 2^30 bytes.
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 28

answer.explanation: Thirty-two address bits identify 2^32 distinct locations. With one byte per location, that is 2^32 bytes, or four units of 2^30 bytes. The selected option is therefore four GB under the explicitly stated binary convention, more precisely four GiB.
