Data-bus width is irrelevant to this location count, and without byte addressing the same number of address bits would not determine a byte capacity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two binary gigabytes would require only 2^31 byte locations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 2^32 byte locations equal four units of 2^30 bytes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Eight binary gigabytes would require 33 address bits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixteen binary gigabytes would require 34 address bits.

evidence.quote: With a address bits there are 2^a addressable locations.
Multiply by bytes per location before calling this a byte capacity.

questions.stem: The control bus in a computer system carries:

options.label: C
options.text: Signals that regulate operations like read/write timing

questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 29

answer.text: Control signals coordinate operations, including read/write timing.
answer.explanation: COA12 defines control signals as coordinating read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements. C expresses that general role. The data and address alternatives belong to distinct signal groups. Interrupt requests may be part of aggregate control, but the word only makes D too restrictive because read/write and timing controls are also included.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actual transferred data belongs to the data bus rather than the control-signal group.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Location selection belongs to address signals rather than the control bus’s coordination role.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Read/write coordination and timing are explicitly among the functions assigned to control signals.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Interrupt requests are only one possible control input; the bus also carries other coordination signals.

evidence.quote: Address signals select a location; data signals carry values; control signals coordinate read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements.
Aggregate control signals include both CPU outputs and device inputs; both data and control buses can therefore be bidirectional under that scope.

questions.stem: In instruction format terminology, an 'opcode' refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: The memory address of the next instruction

options.label: B
options.text: The bits specifying the operation to perform

questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 30

answer.explanation: COA16 defines the opcode as the operation-specifying field. Operand fields locate registers/data and mode fields explain their interpretation. Thus B names the correct format role; next-instruction addresses, result-register identity and operand values are separate quantities. Their presence elsewhere in a machine does not change what opcode means.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Next-instruction position is a PC/control-flow role, not the opcode’s operation-selection role.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Opcode bits select the operation the processor should perform for the instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Result-register selection belongs to an operand/destination field rather than defining the opcode.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An operand data value is distinct from the code selecting the operation to apply.

evidence.quote: An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation.

questions.stem: A zero-address instruction format relies on:
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 31

answer.explanation: COA16 says zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands. The absence of written operand addresses therefore relies on stack organization, not immediate constants or direct memory fields. Generic implicit register addressing is too broad and does not identify the stack discipline specified for this format; PUSH/POP may still have explicit addresses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Implicit register addressing alone does not identify the stack operand convention defining zero-address arithmetic here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Operands come implicitly from the top of the stack, so arithmetic needs no explicit operand-address fields.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Immediate values require encoded operand information; zero-address stack arithmetic is not restricted to constants.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct memory addressing would use an explicit operand address, contrary to the stated zero-address arithmetic format.

evidence.quote: Zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands.
PUSH and POP may still contain an explicit address even on a stack machine.

questions.stem: Which instruction format is most expressive, allowing operations on three separate operands?
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 32

answer.explanation: COA16 defines three-address ADD X,Y,Z as X←Y+Z, allowing a separately named destination and two sources. This matches the stem’s three separate operands. Two-address form overwrites one source, one-address uses an implicit accumulator, and zero-address uses stack operands. Most expressive is interpreted here through the explicit three-operand criterion rather than a universal comparison of complete instruction sets.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Zero-address arithmetic names no explicit operands and instead uses the implicit stack top.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One-address accumulator arithmetic names only one explicit operand and relies on an implicit accumulator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two-address arithmetic overwrites a named source and lacks a separately named third operand field.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Three explicit fields allow one destination and two independently named source operands.

evidence.quote: Three-address ADD X,Y,Z means X←Y+Z under destination-first notation.
Two-address ADD X,Y overwrites X with X+Y.
One-address accumulator ADD X means AC←AC+M[X].
Zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands.

questions.stem: Stack organization follows which principle?
questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 33

answer.explanation: COA17 defines a stack as last-in, first-out: PUSH adds at the logical top and POP removes that top item. The most recently pushed remaining item is therefore the next removed. FIFO describes queue ordering, while arbitrary indexed access or priority selection does not define the stack discipline.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FIFO removes the oldest inserted item, the opposite order from normal stack removal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The last item pushed becomes the top and is the first item popped.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Random access does not enforce removal of the most recently pushed remaining item.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Stack removal follows insertion order in reverse, not a priority ranking assigned to items.

evidence.quote: A stack is last-in, first-out.
PUSH adds an item and POP removes the logical top.

questions.stem: In indirect addressing mode, the instruction contains:

options.label: B
options.text: The direct memory address of the data

options.label: C
options.text: A pointer to the memory address where data resides

questions.hint: Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 34

answer.text: A reference whose stored contents supply the effective address.
answer.explanation: COA18 defines memory-indirect addressing as EA=M[A], followed by operand M[EA]. Thus the instruction’s field identifies a pointer location rather than directly containing the operand value or final operand address. C is the pointer/indirection description. A describes immediate, B direct, and a plain register number identifies a register-based mode rather than this memory-indirect convention.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An actual value encoded in the instruction is immediate addressing rather than memory indirection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Using the field directly as the operand’s address is direct addressing, without the intermediate pointer lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The field identifies a pointer-bearing location; its contents supply the address of the operand data.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A register number names register-based addressing rather than the memory-indirect field defined here.

evidence.quote: Let A be an instruction field, R a register value and M[x] the contents at x.
Immediate uses value A; direct uses EA=A and operand M[A]; indirect uses EA=M[A] then operand M[EA].
Register uses operand R; register-indirect uses EA=R.

questions.stem: Which is a textbook RISC design tendency, without claiming every instruction has single-cycle latency?

options.label: C
options.text: Simple operations, regular encodings and load/store memory access

questions.hint: Compare textbook design tendencies without turning them into guarantees about every processor.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 35

answer.text: Simple operations, regular encodings and load/store memory access
answer.explanation: Textbook RISC emphasizes simple operations, regular encodings, load/store memory access and pipeline-friendly control. These tendencies do not imply every instruction completes with one-cycle latency; steady-state pipeline throughput is a separate measure. Variable lengths and complex operations are associated with CISC tendencies, while an instruction-count range is not a defining guarantee. The choice states these RISC characteristics without imposing a universal single-cycle latency.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Variable lengths are associated with CISC tendencies rather than the stated RISC summary.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This numerical instruction-count range is not the supported RISC characteristic.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: These are the RISC design tendencies named in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Complex microcode control is not the stated RISC design tendency.

evidence.quote: Textbook RISC emphasizes simple operations, regular encodings, load/store memory access, plentiful registers and pipeline-friendly control.
CISC commonly supplies more complex operations, richer addressing modes and variable lengths.
One instruction completing per pipeline cycle is throughput, not proof that every instruction has one-cycle latency.

questions.stem: CISC processors differ from RISC processors primarily in that CISC:

options.label: C
options.text: Supports complex instructions that may take multiple cycles

questions.hint: Compare textbook design tendencies without turning them into guarantees about every processor.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 36

answer.text: CISC commonly supports richer complex instructions, potentially with multi-cycle execution.
answer.explanation: COA20 associates CISC with complex operations, richer addressing and variable lengths, and rejects universal one-cycle latency claims. C therefore gives the matching tendency and permits, rather than requires, multi-cycle execution. The remaining claims either reverse the usual complexity contrast or impose unsupported only/no restrictions. The answer does not claim modern RISC instructions can never take multiple cycles.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fewer instructions reverses the usual simple-versus-rich instruction-set contrast rather than stating the note’s CISC tendency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Only register-to-register operations contradicts the richer addressing modes associated with CISC in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Complex operations and possible multi-cycle latency fit the CISC tendency without claiming exclusivity of multi-cycle execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note does not define CISC by absence of microcode; control implementation is a separate design dimension.

evidence.quote: Textbook RISC emphasizes simple operations, regular encodings, load/store memory access, plentiful registers and pipeline-friendly control.
CISC commonly supplies more complex operations, richer addressing modes and variable lengths.
Modern RISC instructions can take multiple cycles and modern CISC processors can translate instructions into simpler internal operations.

questions.stem: A RISC processor typically has more ______ compared to a CISC processor to compensate for simpler instructions:
questions.hint: Compare textbook design tendencies without turning them into guarantees about every processor.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 37

answer.explanation: COA20 explicitly lists plentiful registers among textbook RISC characteristics, alongside load/store access and simple operations. C is therefore the supported tendency. More addressing modes and instruction bytes are not the stated compensating mechanism, and more cycles per instruction is not a defining guarantee. The typically qualifier matters because the labels alone do not impose a register count on every implementation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: More cycles per instruction is not the plentiful-register mechanism or a guaranteed RISC property.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Richer addressing modes are associated with CISC tendencies, not the stated RISC compensating feature.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Plentiful registers are explicitly one of the textbook RISC traits named by the complete note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: More instruction bytes is not the feature identified as supporting simple RISC operations.

evidence.quote: Textbook RISC emphasizes simple operations, regular encodings, load/store memory access, plentiful registers and pipeline-friendly control.
RISC means Reduced Instruction Set Computer; CISC means Complex Instruction Set Computer.

questions.stem: In Programmed I/O, how does the CPU know when the I/O device has finished its operation?

options.label: A
options.text: The I/O device sends an interrupt signal

options.label: B
options.text: The CPU periodically polls (checks) the status register

options.label: D
options.text: The operating system schedules a check

questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 38

answer.explanation: COA30 defines programmed/polled I/O as repeatedly checking device status while the CPU moves each item. B names that readiness/completion checking mechanism. Interrupt notification belongs to interrupt-driven I/O, and a DMA controller is a separate transfer mechanism. The OS may arrange when polling code runs, but that broad scheduling statement does not replace the actual status check.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An interrupt signal names interrupt-driven notification rather than programmed I/O’s polling mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The CPU reads device status repeatedly to determine readiness or completion in programmed I/O.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DMA-controller completion notification belongs to a DMA transfer rather than programmed CPU-driven I/O.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Scheduling a check is broader software organization; polling the status register is the actual completion-detection method.

evidence.quote: Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.
DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.

questions.stem: The main advantage of Interrupt-Driven I/O over Programmed I/O is:

options.label: B
options.text: The CPU can perform other tasks while waiting for I/O

options.label: D
options.text: It eliminates the need for device drivers

questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 39

answer.text: The CPU can do other work while the device operates.
answer.explanation: COA30 says interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device requests service. That removes continuous status polling, which is the principal advantage in B. Service still consumes CPU time and needs device support/software. Therefore it does not universally increase device transfer speed, eliminate hardware requirements or remove drivers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Avoiding polling does not by itself guarantee that the device or bus transfers data at a higher rate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The CPU can execute other useful work between setup and the device’s service request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interrupt notification requires suitable device/controller support; the note does not promise no special hardware.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A handler/driver must still service the device; interrupt-driven operation does not remove that software role.

evidence.quote: Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.
A controller is hardware; a driver is software that operates it.
Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.

questions.stem: Direct Memory Access (DMA) primarily improves performance by:

options.label: B
options.text: Allowing a controller to transfer data between an I/O device and memory without the CPU copying each word

questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 40

answer.text: Allowing a controller to transfer data between an I/O device and memory without the CPU copying each word
answer.explanation: DMA transfers a block directly between an I/O device and memory after CPU setup. Its performance benefit is reduced per-word CPU copying, leaving the processor available for other work while the controller performs the transfer. CPU configuration and completion handling remain necessary, and DMA still consumes memory bandwidth. It does not inherently raise the clock, compress data or require a faster bus.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DMA changes who performs transfer work, not the processor’s clock frequency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The controller moves the block after setup, avoiding a CPU copy operation for every transferred word.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Data compression is not part of the DMA definition or its stated per-word CPU-work reduction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DMA may use the existing bus and does not inherently replace it with a faster one.

evidence.quote: DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.
DMA does not eliminate CPU involvement in configuration, ownership, address mapping or completion.
DMA reduces per-word CPU work but competes for memory bandwidth.

questions.stem: In Memory-Mapped I/O, how are I/O devices accessed?

options.label: B
options.text: Through dedicated I/O ports separate from memory

options.label: C
options.text: By assigning memory addresses to I/O registers, accessed like regular memory

questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 41

answer.text: Device registers occupy memory addresses and use suitable memory access instructions.
answer.explanation: COA31 says memory-mapped I/O assigns device registers addresses in the memory address space and uses suitable loads/stores. C matches, but like regular memory refers to address/instruction access rather than identical side effects: MMIO widths, ordering and status-read behavior still matter. Special IN/OUT and a separate port space instead describe isolated I/O; DMA is independent of address-space choice.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Special IN/OUT instructions describe isolated/port-mapped I/O rather than the defining memory-mapped access mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A separate port space is the isolated I/O arrangement, not device registers in memory address space.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: MMIO places device registers at memory-space addresses accessed through suitable loads/stores, with device-specific side-effect rules.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: MMIO specifies addressing and access, not an exclusive requirement to transfer all device data through DMA.

evidence.quote: Memory-mapped I/O assigns device registers addresses in the memory address space and uses suitable load/store operations.
Isolated/port-mapped I/O has a separate port space and special instructions such as IN/OUT.
MMIO must respect device access widths, ordering and side effects; a status read is not necessarily a harmless RAM read.

questions.stem: An I/O 'Write Command' instructs the I/O module to:

options.label: A
options.text: Read data from the peripheral and store it in a buffer

options.label: B
options.text: Check the device status for errors

options.label: C
options.text: Take data from the data bus and transmit it to the peripheral

questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 42

answer.text: Transmit system data to the peripheral.
answer.explanation: COA29 defines write/output commands as sending system data to the device. C matches that direction: data from the system bus is handed to the peripheral. Reading brings device data toward the system, status testing inspects readiness/errors, and reset is a control action. These are distinct command functions even when one controller implements them all.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Moving peripheral data into a system buffer is the input/read direction rather than write/output.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checking readiness or errors is a test/status command rather than transferring output data.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A write/output command sends data from the system side to the peripheral device.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reset is a device-control action, not the ordinary data-output direction defining a write command.

evidence.quote: Control commands start actions, test/status commands inspect readiness or errors, read commands bring device data toward the system, and write/output commands send system data to the device.

questions.stem: Which I/O technique is most efficient for transferring large blocks of data, such as disk reads?
questions.hint: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 43

answer.explanation: COA30 explicitly recommends DMA for substantial blocks because it reduces per-word CPU work to setup and completion duties. This matches disk-like large transfers. Polling and interrupt transfer still involve CPU servicing of individual items, while memory-mapped I/O is an address-space design choice that may coexist with DMA. The answer assumes the substantial-block context, not a universal fastest mechanism for every tiny transfer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Programmed I/O makes the CPU check status and move each item, adding substantial work for large blocks.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Interrupt-driven transfer avoids continuous polling but still consumes CPU service work for transferred items.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DMA replaces much per-item CPU work with block setup/completion, matching the substantial-transfer recommendation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory mapping specifies device addressing and can coexist with DMA; it does not itself offload block movement.

evidence.quote: Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.
DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.
Choose it for substantial blocks; mapping devices to addresses is a separate design dimension.

questions.stem: SMP (Symmetric Multiprocessing) systems are characterized by:

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple different processors with specialized roles

options.label: B
options.text: Compatible peer processors sharing memory and I/O under one operating system

options.label: C
options.text: Processors with separate private address spaces communicating by messages

options.label: D
options.text: Independent networked computers without shared memory

questions.hint: Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 44

answer.text: Compatible peer processors sharing memory and I/O under one operating system
answer.explanation: SMP gives processors peer roles with shared memory and I/O under an operating system. Compatibility and symmetric roles matter; every physical processor property need not be identical. Specialized asymmetric roles do not state that model, while separate address spaces and independent networked computers describe distributed organization. The alternatives compare coherent organizations without an impossible single-processor multi-chip description.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Specialized unequal processor roles describe an asymmetric organization rather than the peer-role model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Peer roles with shared memory and I/O under one OS match the SMP definition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Separate private address spaces and message communication describe distributed-memory organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Independent computers without shared memory do not have the stated SMP shared-memory organization.

evidence.quote: SMP processors share memory/I/O and have peer roles under an OS.
Distributed-memory systems communicate between separate address spaces.

questions.stem: Pipelining improves CPU performance by:

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing the clock speed of each stage

options.label: B
options.text: Executing one instruction at a time faster

options.label: C
options.text: Overlapping the execution stages of multiple instructions simultaneously

questions.hint: Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 45

answer.explanation: COA35 defines pipelining by overlapping stages from different instructions and says it primarily improves throughput. C directly states that mechanism. It does not require faster stages, larger registers or a single instruction completing all work faster. Pipeline fill/drain, stalls and the slowest stage constrain actual gains, so overlap rather than guaranteed latency reduction is the supported explanation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pipeline performance does not require increasing each stage’s clock speed; clock choice is limited by the slowest stage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An instruction still spans several stages, so lower single-instruction latency is not the defining improvement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Overlapping stages lets different instructions progress concurrently, increasing completed-work throughput.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Larger register width does not define stage overlap or directly explain pipelining’s throughput benefit.

evidence.quote: A pipeline overlaps stages of different instructions; it primarily improves throughput.
The ideal steady-state completion rate is one instruction per cycle, while an individual instruction still spans multiple stages.

questions.stem: In an arithmetic pipeline for floating-point addition, which is the FIRST sub-operation performed?
questions.hint: Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 46

answer.explanation: COA10 orders floating addition as compare exponents, shift the smaller significand to align, add/subtract, normalize and round. Comparing exponents must precede alignment because their difference determines the required shift. Adding before alignment combines unequal place weights, and normalization happens after arithmetic. Therefore D is the first named sub-operation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normalization follows aligned addition/subtraction rather than initiating the floating-point addition sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Significands must first be aligned to a common exponent before their values can be added correctly.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Alignment follows exponent comparison, which determines which significand to shift and by how much.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Exponent comparison is explicitly first and supplies the information needed for subsequent alignment.

evidence.quote: For floating addition, compare exponents, shift the smaller significand to align, add or subtract, normalize and round.

questions.stem: Which statement describes vector-instruction semantics rather than guaranteeing simultaneous execution of every array element?

options.label: A
options.text: Processes one element at a time faster

options.label: B
options.text: One vector instruction applies an operation across multiple data elements, possibly in lane-sized batches

options.label: D
options.text: Operates at a higher clock frequency

questions.hint: Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 47

answer.text: One vector instruction applies an operation across multiple data elements, possibly in lane-sized batches
answer.explanation: A vector instruction describes an operation over a sequence of elements. Its semantics cover multiple data elements, but physical lanes can process those elements in batches instead of executing the entire array at one instant. The choice distinguishes vector from scalar processing without requiring simultaneous execution of every element. Faster individual elements, fewer transistors or a higher clock are implementation properties rather than definitions of vector processing.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Faster scalar element processing does not define vector semantics.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This states the multi-element instruction semantics while permitting physical batching.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A transistor-count reduction is not part of the definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A higher clock frequency is not required by vector semantics.

evidence.quote: A vector instruction describes an operation over a sequence of elements; physical lanes may process them in batches, not all in one instant.

questions.stem: For an ideal single-issue RISC pipeline in steady state after filling, with balanced stages and no stalls, what is the completion throughput?

options.label: A
options.text: One instruction per two clock cycles

questions.hint: Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 48

answer.explanation: An ideal single-issue pipeline overlaps stages of successive instructions. After filling, it completes one instruction each cycle when stages are balanced and no hazards or other stalls interfere. An individual instruction still crosses several stages, so this is throughput rather than one-cycle instruction latency. Specifying single issue excludes a superscalar interpretation that could complete more than one instruction per cycle.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One completion per two cycles is below the stated ideal no-stall rate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The ideal steady-state single-issue completion rate is one per cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two per cycle requires multiple-issue resources beyond the stated design.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The ideal rate follows from the specified single-issue pipeline assumptions.

evidence.quote: In an ideal k-stage single-issue pipeline, n instructions take k+n−1 cycles when stages are balanced and there are no stalls.
The ideal steady-state completion rate is one instruction per cycle, while an individual instruction still spans multiple stages.

questions.stem: Flynn's taxonomy classifies parallel computer architectures based on:

options.label: A
options.text: Number of processors and memory size

questions.hint: Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 49

answer.explanation: COA37 explicitly defines Flynn classification by instruction and data streams. SISD has one of each, SIMD one instruction stream with multiple data elements, and MIMD multiple streams of each. Processor count, capacity, clock and register/cache sizes are implementation properties rather than the two classification axes. Therefore B directly matches the taxonomy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Processor count and memory size do not define the instruction-stream/data-stream axes of Flynn’s taxonomy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Flynn classifies the number of instruction streams and data streams, producing SISD/SIMD/MISD/MIMD categories.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Clock and bus width measure implementation characteristics rather than Flynn’s stream-count classification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cache capacity and register count are not the two axes used by Flynn’s taxonomy.

evidence.quote: Flynn classifies instruction and data streams: SISD has one of each; SIMD applies one instruction stream to multiple data elements; MIMD uses multiple instruction and data streams; MISD has multiple instruction streams for a common data stream and is uncommon.

questions.stem: The primary goal of parallel processing is to increase:

options.label: C
options.text: Throughput — the amount of processing per unit time

questions.hint: Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model.
sources: Computer Organization & Architecture review questions · Question 50

answer.text: Throughput: completed processing per unit time.
answer.explanation: COA37 says more cores increase available parallel work while serial dependencies and coordination limit speedup. COA34 defines throughput as completed work per unit time. Parallel processing aims to raise that work rate, matching C, rather than inherently increasing physical memory, clock frequency or register width. Actual gains still depend on enough independent work and manageable overhead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Parallel execution does not inherently increase the system’s installed memory capacity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Additional concurrent work can improve throughput without increasing any processor’s clock frequency.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent useful work aims to increase completed processing per unit time, subject to serial and coordination limits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Register width is an architectural data-size property, not the primary objective of parallel execution.

evidence.quote: More cores increase available parallel work, but serial dependencies and coordination limit speedup.
Throughput counts completed work per unit time; latency measures one job’s delay.

blocks.text: Architecture describes programmer-visible behavior: instructions, registers, data types, address spaces and I/O conventions.
Organization is the implementation: control signals, internal buses, pipelines and memory technology.
Different organizations can implement the same architecture; neither definition imposes a maximum lifetime.
Microarchitecture names the internal processor design.
CPU, main memory, I/O and their interconnection are the major structural parts.
The CPU contains an ALU, control unit and registers; a microcontroller is a complete integrated control system, not another mandatory CPU subunit.
A motherboard physically connects components.
Gates are fundamental logic building blocks; distinguish that level from CPU, memory, disk and motherboard components.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
In the textbook Von Neumann model, instructions and data share an addressed memory system; the CPU normally advances sequentially unless control flow changes.
Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths.
Modern systems may combine a unified address-space view with separate instruction/data caches, so “architecture used nowadays” is not an exclusive choice.
Separate program/data regions within one memory do not make a Harvard machine.
An operating system manages resources and provides services.
Applications solve user tasks.
A compiler translates source into target code; assembly is a symbolic form of machine instructions.
JIT compilation happens during program execution, often translating intermediate code.
Translation before execution alone does not distinguish JIT from an ahead-of-time compiler.
Machine-language programming depends on the register set, supported types and memory/addressing structure.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR is 1 if any input is 1.
NOT complements a bit.
NAND complements AND; NOR complements OR.
For two inputs XOR is 1 when inputs differ, and XNOR when they agree.
An enabled buffer copies its input.
A bubble at a gate output indicates inversion: an AND-shaped symbol with a bubble is NAND.
With n binary inputs, enumerate 2^n truth-table rows.
Evaluate complements, products and then sums.
A plus sign means Boolean OR, not integer addition.
Worked microexample

items.text: F=x+y'z at x=0,y=1,z=1: y'=0, so F=0 OR (0 AND 1)=0. Four independent inputs give 16 rows.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
Useful identities are A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A, AA=A, A+A'=1, AA'=0, A+AB=A and A(A+B)=A. De Morgan gives (AB)'=A'+B' and (A+B)'=A'B'.
Check a proposed simplification with a truth table if uncertain.
NAND and NOR are each universal: feeding the same input to both inputs constructs NOT; combine complemented gates to construct AND or OR.
For Karnaugh maps, use Gray-code order, group adjacent 1s in rectangles of powers of two, allow wraparound and overlap, cover every required 1, and remove variables changing within a group.
Do not group diagonally or include a required 0.
Worked microexample

items.text: AB+AB'=A(B+B')=A. A NAND A=A'; NAND followed by inversion gives AND.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
A combinational output depends on present inputs after propagation delay.
Adders, multiplexers, demultiplexers, encoders and decoders have no stored logical state.
A sequential circuit depends on stored state as well as inputs; registers, counters and flip-flops are examples.
This is the defensible criterion when comparing a shift register against decoder, encoder and multiplexer.
A flip-flop stores one bit while powered.
State retention during operation does not mean nonvolatile storage.
Ordinary flip-flops and SRAM lose state when power is removed.
Clocked sequential circuits update at designated clock events; combinational logic does not inherently require a clock.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
For an active-high SR latch, S=1,R=0 sets, S=0,R=1 resets, and S=R=0 holds; S=R=1 is forbidden for the NOR-latch model.
Active-low NAND-latch conventions differ.
A D flip-flop copies D at its active edge.
JK holds for 00, resets for 01, sets for 10 and toggles for 11.
T toggles when T=1 and holds when T=0.
Trace a sequential circuit one clock at a time from the given initial state.
A k-bit binary counter has 2^k states and wraps modulo 2^k unless extra control changes the sequence.
Ripple counters propagate changes asynchronously; synchronous counters share a clock.
Worked microexample

items.text: A 3-bit counter at 110 advances to 111, then 000. A T flip-flop starting at 0 with T inputs 1,0,1 gives states 1,1,0.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
A half-adder has sum A XOR B and carry AB.
A full-adder includes carry-in: sum=A XOR B XOR Cin and carry=AB+Cin(A XOR B).
Cascading full-adders propagates carry across a word.
A 2^k-to-1 multiplexer uses k select bits to choose one data input.
A demultiplexer routes one input to a selected output.
A k-to-2^k decoder asserts the selected output, subject to enable and active-level conventions.
An ordinary encoder assumes one active input; a priority encoder defines which wins if several are active.
Registers are storage, not combinational code converters.
Worked microexample

items.text: For a full-adder with A=B=Cin=1, binary total is 11: sum=1 and carry=1. An 8-to-1 mux needs 3 select bits.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
In base b, a digit at position i has value digit×b^i. Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.
Convert a positive integer to binary by repeated division by 2 and read remainders upward.
For fractions, repeatedly multiply by 2 and read integer parts downward.
Group binary bits in threes for octal and fours for hexadecimal, outward from the radix point.
BCD encodes each decimal digit separately in four bits; BCD 12 is 0001 0010, while ordinary binary 12 is 1100.
ASCII is a character code, not a physical I/O interface.
Worked microexample

items.text: 1011₂=8+2+1=11. 2F₁₆=47. 101.101₂=5.625. Decimal 13 gives remainders 1,0,1,1 and hence 1101₂.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
For n-bit unsigned values the range is 0 through 2^n−1.
Two’s complement ranges from −2^(n−1) through 2^(n−1)−1.
Negate by inverting all n bits and adding one.
Compute A−B as A+(two’s complement of B), retaining n result bits.
Signed magnitude and one’s complement have two zero encodings; two’s complement has one.
Unsigned carry and signed overflow are different.
Signed addition overflows when equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result.
Keep the width fixed throughout the calculation.
Worked microexample

items.text: In 4 bits, 7−3 = 0111+1101 = 1 0100; discard carry to get 4. But 0111+0001=1000 is signed overflow, since +8 is outside −8…+7.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
A normalized binary floating-point value is sign×significand×2^exponent.
For ordinary IEEE binary32 normal values, value=(−1)^s(1.f)2^(e−127); binary64 uses 11 exponent bits and bias 1023.
Special exponent patterns represent zero/subnormal values or infinities/NaNs, so the implicit leading 1 is not universal.
For floating addition, compare exponents, shift the smaller significand to align, add or subtract, normalize and round.
Alignment may lose low-order bits.
Overflow concerns exponent range; rounding error concerns finite precision.
An arithmetic pipeline overlaps these steps for different operand pairs; it need not perform all steps in one cycle.
Worked microexample
Computer Organization and Architecture module

notes.title: Register transfers, buses and memory cycles

blocks.text: R2←R1 copies R1 into R2; it does not erase R1.
A control condition P:R2←R1 performs the transfer only when P is true at the relevant clock event.
Simultaneous transfers read old register values; sequential statements can use a newly written value.
A common bus selects one source at a time, while destination load signals select receivers.
A read places an address in MAR/AR, asserts read, waits for memory and captures data in MDR/MBR/DR. A write supplies both address and data and asserts write.
The ALU computes; the control unit sequences and enables the transfers.
A microoperation is one elementary operation on register contents.
Worked microexample

items.text: With R1=3,R2=7, simultaneous R1←R2,R2←R1 swaps to 7,3. Executed sequentially, both end at 7.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
Address signals select a location; data signals carry values; control signals coordinate read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements.
In the simple CPU-master model, addresses flow from CPU to memory, while data travels in either direction.
A DMA controller can also become bus master.
Aggregate control signals include both CPU outputs and device inputs; both data and control buses can therefore be bidirectional under that scope.
With a address bits there are 2^a addressable locations.
Multiply by bytes per location before calling this a byte capacity.
Word width, data-bus width, instruction width and address width need not match.
Worked microexample

items.text: 32 address bits and byte addressing give 2^32 bytes=4 GiB (often called 4 GB in introductory questions). A 16-bit data bus does not itself imply a 16-bit address space.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
To set selected bits use A OR mask; to clear them use A AND NOT(mask); to toggle use A XOR mask; to retain only selected bits use A AND mask.
A XOR A clears the entire register.
Clearing with XOR is valid only with the appropriate operand, not any arbitrary mask.
Logical shifts insert zero.
Arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit.
Left shift inserts zero and may overflow; it does not preserve the sign in every case.
Rotate returns a shifted-out bit at the opposite end.
SISO shift registers delay serial streams; SIPO collects a word and PISO serializes a parallel word.
Worked microexample

items.text: A=1010, mask=1100: set→1110, selective clear→0010, toggle→0110. Arithmetic-right 1100 gives 1110 (−4 to −2 in two’s complement); logical-right gives 0110.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
PC identifies the next instruction to fetch.
IR holds the fetched instruction; MAR holds an address used for the current memory access; MDR holds transferred data.
The accumulator holds operands/results, SP tracks the stack, and status flags report conditions. “Address of the instruction” without a phase can describe PC or MAR.
Registers and cache both store temporary information, but registers are explicit execution operands and cache holds copies of memory blocks.
A control word chooses ALU sources, destination and operation.
Use the machine’s encoding table rather than guessing opcodes.
In this 14-bit control-word example, SELA, SELB and SELD each have 3 bits, followed by a 5-bit operation field.
Worked microexample

items.text: For R1←R2−R3 in this encoding, select 010,011,001 and subtraction 00101: 010 011 001 00101. Source and destination order matters.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module

notes.title: Fetch, decode, execute and next-PC choice

blocks.text: A conceptual instruction cycle fetches an instruction, decodes opcode/addressing fields, obtains operands, executes, writes results where required and checks permitted interrupts.
A five-stage implementation may name stages IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB; these stages are not mandatory for every architecture.
A sample fetch is MAR←PC; MDR←M[MAR]; IR←MDR; PC←PC+instruction_length.
A branch can replace the sequential PC later.
Thus “which phase determines the next instruction?” needs to distinguish reading the current PC from calculating a branch target.
The control unit coordinates fetching and data flow; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic.
A write-back/result-storage phase is not another fetch.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation.
A 4-bit opcode permits at most 16 encodings, not necessarily 16 implemented instructions.
A 6-bit operand-reference field has 64 encodings; what they designate depends on the machine.
Three-address ADD X,Y,Z means X←Y+Z under destination-first notation.
Two-address ADD X,Y overwrites X with X+Y. One-address accumulator ADD X means AC←AC+M[X].
Zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands.
Count explicit operand fields; an instruction such as INC X does not become an accumulator instruction merely because it has one written operand.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
A stack is last-in, first-out.
PUSH adds an item and POP removes the logical top.
A register stack uses registers; a memory stack uses RAM and a stack pointer.
Check whether SP points to the top or the next free location, whether addresses increase or decrease, and whether the update occurs before or after access.
Overflow means pushing a full stack; underflow means popping an empty one.
Zero-address arithmetic typically pops the second operand first, then the first operand; subtraction therefore needs careful order.
PUSH and POP may still contain an explicit address even on a stack machine.
Worked microexample

items.text: For (A+B)×(C+D): PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; PUSH C; PUSH D; ADD; MUL. For a downward-growing full stack, PUSH commonly decrements SP before storing and POP reads before incrementing.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
Let A be an instruction field, R a register value and M[x] the contents at x. Immediate uses value A; direct uses EA=A and operand M[A]; indirect uses EA=M[A] then operand M[EA].
Register uses operand R; register-indirect uses EA=R. Indexed/base displacement uses EA=R+A; PC-relative uses the architecture-defined PC plus a signed displacement.
Auto-increment/decrement also updates the register by operand size.
A transfer between a register and memory does not uniquely specify addressing mode; either direct, indexed or indirect addressing may produce it.
Worked microexample

items.text: A=100,R=20,M[100]=300,M[300]=9: direct operand is 300; indirect operand is 9; indexed EA is 120. An immediate field 100 is the value 100, not M[100].

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
Data-transfer instructions copy values.
Arithmetic/logic instructions compute values.
TEST/CMP examine values and set condition information, often without retaining the arithmetic result.
Branch instructions choose a target, conditionally or unconditionally.
CALL saves a return point; RETURN restores it.
SKIP, where supported, bypasses the next instruction when its condition holds. “Jump to the next instruction” does not clearly mean skip.
External interrupts arise from devices or timers; synchronous internal exceptions arise from the executing instruction, such as divide errors, illegal opcodes or access violations.
A software interrupt is deliberately requested by an instruction.
Arithmetic overflow trapping depends on architecture and instruction; ordinary overflow flags need not trigger an interrupt.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
Textbook RISC emphasizes simple operations, regular encodings, load/store memory access, plentiful registers and pipeline-friendly control.
CISC commonly supplies more complex operations, richer addressing modes and variable lengths.
Hardwired control directly generates control signals; microprogrammed control sequences stored control words.
These are tendencies, not universal guarantees.
One instruction completing per pipeline cycle is throughput, not proof that every instruction has one-cycle latency.
Modern RISC instructions can take multiple cycles and modern CISC processors can translate instructions into simpler internal operations.
Neither label guarantees lower power, cost or execution time.
The semantic gap is the distance between high-level constructs and machine operations; reducing it is associated with richer instructions, not a universal shared objective of both design approaches.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
In Intel x86 notation, AX/BX/CX/DX, BP/SP and SI/DI are 16-bit general-purpose registers, with conventional special roles.
AL is AX’s low byte and AH its high byte; analogous byte names apply to BX/CX/DX.
EAX is 32-bit and RAX 64-bit.
FLAGS/EFLAGS/RFLAGS report status; IP/EIP/RIP identifies instruction position.
CS and SS are code/stack segment registers.
DX is programmer-visible; IR/MDR are conceptual internal registers.
SP’s stack role does not remove it from Intel’s general-purpose register classification.
EAX/EIP existed with the 80386, before Pentium; R8–R15 belong to the 64-bit extension, not original Pentium.
State the textbook convention when using a narrower “multipurpose” register category.
Intel Software Developer Manual, Volume 1

notes.title: x86 instruction legality and implicit operands

blocks.text: Assume Intel destination-first syntax and ordinary legacy x86 forms.
MOV AL,BP is invalid because operand widths differ (8 versus 16 bits).
INC CX and DEC CX are valid word operations.
Segment-register MOV has register/memory forms, not a direct immediate-to-segment form: load an immediate into AX, then MOV DS,AX.
Unsigned MUL with a byte operand multiplies AL by that byte and writes AX.
With a word operand it multiplies AX and writes DX:AX.
Thus AL=8 and BH=10 gives AX=80 after MUL BH; CL is irrelevant.
MOVS and LODS are string transfer operations, XCHG exchanges operands, and INC is arithmetic. “Different” requires the transfer-versus-arithmetic criterion.
Intel Software Developer Manual, Volume 2B
A usual speed/cost-per-bit order is registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, DRAM, SSD, HDD and archival tape.
Faster levels are generally smaller and more expensive per bit.
Access time measures latency of a read/write; cycle time is the minimum interval before another operation and may include recovery.
Transfer rate measures data per time, not individual-request delay.
Temporal locality reuses recent data; spatial locality uses nearby locations.
Cache copies memory blocks near the CPU.
Hit ratio=hits/accesses; miss ratio=1−hit ratio.
Distinguish capacity, latency, bandwidth and hit ratio before comparing alternatives.
Worked microexample

items.text: For 90 hits in 100 accesses, hit ratio=0.9. If hit time is 2 ns and an additional miss penalty is 50 ns, AMAT=2+0.1×50=7 ns.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
SRAM uses powered bistable storage: fast and costly per bit, without periodic refresh.
DRAM stores charge and requires refresh: denser and commonly used for main memory.
Both are ordinarily volatile.
ROM and flash retain contents without power; erasable/programmed variants mean “ROM can never be modified” is too broad.
Firmware is low-level system code, commonly in nonvolatile storage.
For a chip described as 2^a×w, a is the number of address inputs and w the data width.
Combine chips in parallel to increase word width and in banks to increase the number of words.
Distinguish address decoding from data selection.
Worked microexample

items.text: Eight 1K×1 chips in parallel make 1K×8 storage: 10 shared address lines and 8 data bits. Four such banks make 4K×8 and require 12 address bits overall.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module

notes.title: Cache placement, index bits and conflicts

blocks.text: Let B be block size in bytes and L the number of cache lines.
Block number=floor(address/B); offset=address mod B. Direct mapping uses line=block mod L. Fully associative placement permits any line.
A W-way set-associative cache has S=L/W sets and set=block mod S; any of W ways in that set may hold the block.
For power-of-two sizes, offset bits=log2 B, index bits=log2 S and remaining address bits form the tag.
Compare tags and valid bits to identify a hit.
Two blocks with the same direct-mapped index cannot reside together.
Associations reduce placement conflicts but require more tag comparisons.
Worked microexample

items.text: 16-byte blocks and four direct-mapped lines: addresses 0 and 64 have block numbers 0 and 4, both index 0, so alternating them causes conflict misses.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
FIFO evicts the earliest inserted line; LRU evicts the least recently accessed line.
On each access, record hit/miss, the set involved and policy state.
Hits update LRU order but do not reset FIFO insertion order.
Direct mapping has no replacement choice within a line.
Write-through updates the lower level on each write; write-back modifies cache and marks a dirty bit, writing to the lower level on eviction.
Write-allocate fetches a missed block before writing; no-write-allocate writes below without installing it.
L1/L2 describe hierarchy levels; split cache means separate instruction/data caches and unified means combined.
Internal/external location is another classification, not synonymous with split/unified.
Worked microexample

items.text: Two fully associative lines, references A,B,A,C: all except the second A are misses. LRU evicts B for C; FIFO evicts A.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module

notes.title: Virtual addresses, MMU and page faults

blocks.text: Virtual memory gives processes translated address spaces and protection; backing storage can hold nonresident pages.
The MMU translates virtual/logical addresses to physical addresses, using page tables and often a TLB of recent translations.
Virtual memory is not just extra disk disguised as RAM.
With page size P, page=floor(virtual_address/P), offset=virtual_address mod P and physical_address=frame×P+offset.
A valid nonresident page access faults and may require loading data; invalid or forbidden accesses can also fault.
A cache miss, TLB miss and page fault are different events; not every page fault reads a disk, since zero-fill and already-resident shared pages exist.
Worked microexample

items.text: With 1024-byte pages, address 2053 is page 2, offset 5. If page 2 maps to frame 7, physical address=7173.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
An HDD stores magnetic patterns on tracks divided into sectors; reads/writes access addressed blocks while platters rotate.
A head normally stays over a track while reading but moves radially for seeks.
It does not need continuous power to preserve stored bits.
SSDs use nonvolatile semiconductor storage without mechanical seek.
Optical media use lasers; tape is suited to sequential streaming and archives.
An Ethernet cable is a communication medium, not a disk or RAM.

In textbook access taxonomy, tape is sequential, disk is direct access with positioning delay, RAM is random access with broadly address-independent timing, and associative access matches content. “Random-access disk” is also common informal usage; specify the taxonomy when comparing direct and random access.
Optical access ranges such as 100–300 ms are historical examples, not universal device specifications.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
A peripheral performs input, output or storage outside the CPU’s execution core; CPU itself is not a peripheral.
Input units encode external information and output units present processed results.
A device controller handles device protocol/timing; its interface commonly exposes data, status and control registers.
Buffers absorb speed differences and error/status bits report conditions.

Control commands start actions, test/status commands inspect readiness or errors, read commands bring device data toward the system, and write/output commands send system data to the device. “Issue” describes sending a command, not a standard fourth command category.
A controller is hardware; a driver is software that operates it.
Computer Organization and Architecture module
Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.
DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.
Completion or errors can interrupt the CPU.
DMA does not eliminate CPU involvement in configuration, ownership, address mapping or completion.
Burst mode can hold the bus for a block; cycle stealing takes individual transfer opportunities, and transparent DMA uses idle opportunities.
DMA reduces per-word CPU work but competes for memory bandwidth.
Choose it for substantial blocks; mapping devices to addresses is a separate design dimension.
Worked microexample

items.text: For 1000 words, polling or interrupt transfer may require CPU work per word. DMA replaces much of that work with setup and completion, although the actual memory transfers still take time.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module

notes.title: I/O address spaces, priorities and handshaking

blocks.text: Memory-mapped I/O assigns device registers addresses in the memory address space and uses suitable load/store operations.
Isolated/port-mapped I/O has a separate port space and special instructions such as IN/OUT.
MMIO must respect device access widths, ordering and side effects; a status read is not necessarily a harmless RAM read.

Asynchronous handshaking uses request/ready and acknowledgement signals to tolerate unequal speeds: sender presents data and requests, receiver accepts and acknowledges, then each withdraws its signal.
A single strobe lacks this feedback.
Interrupt priority selects among simultaneous requests, using schemes such as polling, daisy chains or priority hardware.
Serial sends bits over time; parallel transfers multiple bits on multiple lines, without guaranteeing higher real-world speed.
Computer Organization and Architecture module

notes.title: Named interfaces: choose by connection role

blocks.text: USB is a serial peripheral interconnect used by keyboards and external storage; RS-232 specifies a traditional point-to-point serial electrical/interface standard.
Both RS-232 and USB use serial communication; distinguish their interface roles and specifications.
HDMI carries digital video and audio.
Ethernet connects network devices; it is not memory.
SATA is a storage interface; legacy IDE/PATA and SCSI represent other storage connections, while iSCSI carries SCSI commands over IP.

PCI is a peripheral expansion interconnect, not a disk protocol; connecting unlike bus segments requires suitable bridge/controller logic. “Extends processor-bus connectivity” without topology does not uniquely identify PCI or Multibus.
POSIX is a software interface standard with operations such as open/read/write/close; ASCII is a character encoding.
An unqualified “standard PC disk interface” needs an era or device requirement.
USB Implementers Forum, mass storage transport specification
Texas Instruments AN-216
HDMI Licensing Administrator specifications overview
Linux libATA Developer Guide
An ADC measures an analog input and produces a digital code; a DAC produces an analog output from a digital code.
ADC080x parts are 8-bit successive-approximation analog-to-digital converters; DAC0830 is a digital-to-analog converter, while 82C55 denotes a programmable parallel I/O interface, not an ADC.
Component names are not interchangeable with the direction of conversion.
For an ideal n-bit converter spanning a voltage range V, one code step is approximately V/2^n; actual endpoint conventions and specifications must be stated.
Quantization rounds an analog range into discrete codes; sample rate and resolution measure different properties.
Worked microexample

items.text: An ideal 8-bit ADC over a 5.12 V span has 256 codes and a 0.02 V step. Greater bit depth reduces the quantization step for the same span.

blocks.text: Texas Instruments ADC0804-N
CPU time=instruction_count×CPI×clock_period=instruction_count×CPI/clock_rate.
CPI may be a weighted average across instruction classes; IPC is its reciprocal only under a consistent whole-program definition.
Raising clock frequency does not guarantee a faster program when instruction count or stalls increase.
Throughput counts completed work per unit time; latency measures one job’s delay.
When a fraction f of execution is sped up by factor s, overall speedup=1/((1−f)+f/s).
The unaffected fraction limits gains.
Compare the same workload and include memory and branch penalties instead of equating clock speed with performance.
Worked microexample

items.text: 10^6 instructions, CPI=2 and 1 GHz take 2 ms. If half the time becomes twice as fast, overall speedup=1/(0.5+0.25)=4/3, not 2.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
A pipeline overlaps stages of different instructions; it primarily improves throughput.
In an ideal k-stage single-issue pipeline, n instructions take k+n−1 cycles when stages are balanced and there are no stalls.
Without overlap, comparable work takes nk stage cycles.
The ideal steady-state completion rate is one instruction per cycle, while an individual instruction still spans multiple stages.
Choose the pipeline clock using the slowest stage plus register overhead.

Fill/drain overhead matters for short streams. “Fetch/decode one instruction while executing another” describes pipelining, whereas issuing several instructions in one cycle requires multiple-issue resources.
Worked microexample

items.text: A five-stage pipeline processing 10 instructions takes 14 ideal cycles versus 50 without overlap: speedup=50/14≈3.57. It does not reach the limiting factor of five for this short stream.

blocks.text: Computer Organization and Architecture module
Structural hazards compete for one resource.
Data hazards arise when an instruction needs a result not yet available; forwarding can supply results early, but some dependencies still stall.
Control hazards arise when the next PC depends on an unresolved branch.
Branch prediction guesses direction/target and continues speculatively; wrong guesses discard work.
Superscalar execution issues multiple instructions to multiple functional units in a cycle when dependencies permit.
Out-of-order execution schedules ready operations before stalled older ones while preserving architectural results and exception behavior.
Dynamic resource allocation assigns available internal entries/units at runtime.
These mechanisms exploit instruction-level parallelism; wider fetch improves instruction supply, not necessarily individual memory latency.

Flynn classifies instruction and data streams: SISD has one of each; SIMD applies one instruction stream to multiple data elements; MIMD uses multiple instruction and data streams; MISD has multiple instruction streams for a common data stream and is uncommon.
A vector instruction describes an operation over a sequence of elements; physical lanes may process them in batches, not all in one instant.
SMP processors share memory/I/O and have peer roles under an OS.
Distributed-memory systems communicate between separate address spaces.
More cores increase available parallel work, but serial dependencies and coordination limit speedup. “Core i7” is a product family rather than one core count; a model number is essential.

The familiar generation convention associates first with vacuum tubes, second with transistors, third with integrated circuits and fourth with microprocessor/VLSI-era personal computers.
Stored-program machines arose in the first era.
High-level languages became prominent around the transition into the second; introduction dates do not fit every generation boundary.
Magnetic-core memory spanned more than one era, so “witnessed use” cannot identify exactly one.
Several generations improved performance.
Integration generally reduced individual component dimensions while capacity, density and processor performance grew; these are trends rather than guarantees for every model.
Intel’s 80386 introduced 32-bit x86 execution in 1985, before 80486/Pentium; the 80286 was a 16-bit predecessor.
An n-bit processor label does not force its PC, IR or address register to be n bits.

Main memory, registers and cache can all provide temporary storage; identify the scope and role. Memory can also include nonvolatile ROM/flash, so distinguish RAM when comparing power-off data retention with disk storage.
Architecture lifetime, power efficiency and generational improvements require assumptions; definitions alone do not make these exclusive.

Intel’s desktop comparison chart lists the Core i7-920 with four physical cores and eight hardware threads. Core count and thread count are distinct specification fields: use the exact processor model and the field requested rather than inferring a count from the Core i7 family name.

A bus is a set of common signal lines used to transfer binary information among connected units. In a parallel register bus, one line carries each bit position; control signals select a source and enable the intended destination. Storage registers and memory retain information, while the bus provides a transfer path.

In the textbook single-accumulator organization, a memory-reference instruction has an operation part and an address part. The address locates a memory operand; the operation combines that operand with the accumulator as required. The address field is not the operand value itself, and this simple format does not describe every addressing mode or instruction set.
Computer Organization and Architecture module · page 47

RISC means Reduced Instruction Set Computer; CISC means Complex Instruction Set Computer. The textbook RISC design pairs a relatively large register set, load/store access and easily decoded instructions with hardwired rather than microprogrammed control and an efficient pipeline. These are design tendencies, not guarantees of one-cycle latency or lower power for every implementation.

notes.title: Instruction and stack pointers in 64-bit x86

blocks.text: In Intel 64-bit mode, RIP holds the offset of the next instruction to execute. RSP is the 64-bit stack pointer, extending the ESP/SP stack role. These pointers are distinct from CS and SS, which are code and stack segment registers.
Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer’s Manual, Volume 1 · §§3.4–3.5 and 6.1
The circled plus symbol ⊕ denotes exclusive OR. For two Boolean inputs, A⊕B is 1 exactly when the inputs differ; an overbar or output inversion would complement this result.

A flip-flop is bistable: it has two stable states representing 0 and 1. While powered, it can retain one bit until an input or designated clock event changes its state. Multiple flip-flops are required to represent a multi-bit counter state.

Give the four blueprint outcomes equal attention: hardware/software structure, CPU operations, I/O communication and performance enhancement. Use historical architecture facts as a small supplement to the core principles.
